metadata.scope: e_liangyi (261 baronies across k_dali, k_dongchuan, k_kuizhou, k_qianzhong, k_xichuan, k_xingyuan)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_dali_1.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Dali Kingdom and capital name in 937 CE by Duan Siping (recorded in Xin Wudaishi and Songshi, Vol. 488), succeeding the Nanzhao capital of Yangjumie City.
b_dali_1.etymology_analysis: Dali (大理) is a Chinese dynastic and capital name adopted by Duan Siping in 937 CE when he established the Kingdom of Dali at Yangjumie City, signifying 'great governance' or 'great order.'

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) for Han Yeyu County (109 BCE); Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222a) and Manshu (Vol. 6) for Taihe City (739 CE) and Yangjumie City (779 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Erhai basin was established as Yeyu County in 109 BCE, became Nanzhao's Taihe City in 739 CE and Yangjumie City in 779 CE, and was renamed Dali in 937 CE.

b_ningbei.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ningbei Jiedu (宁北节度) by Nanzhao in 794 CE (10th year of Zhenyuan), with its seat at Ningbei City recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222a) and Manshu (Vol. 6).
b_ningbei.etymology_analysis: Ningbei (宁北) is a Nanzhao-era Chinese administrative name meaning 'pacifying the north,' designating the northern frontier commandery on the eastern border of former Han Yeyu County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Manshu (Vol. 6), noting Ningbei City lay in the eastern territory of Han Yeyu County (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Nanzhao's Ningbei City was established on the eastern border of the Han-era Yeyu County.

b_yunnan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 109 BCE (2nd year of Yuanfeng, Western Han) as Yunnan County under Yizhou Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and later as Tang Yunnan Zhou / Yunnan City in Manshu (Vol. 6).
b_yunnan.etymology_analysis: Yunnan (云南, 'south of the clouds') was first attested as a Han county name in 109 BCE at modern Xiangyun (Yunnan驿), later giving its name to the Tang commandery and the province.

b_bipan.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as the Bipan/Mipan tribe (閟畔部), one of the thirty-seven tribes of the Dali Kingdom that submitted to the Mongols in the 13th century (recorded in Yuanshi, Vol. 61).

morphemes.translation: indigenous tribal and place name of the Dongchuan area

b_bipan.etymology_analysis: Bipan (𮤲畔, standard historical form 閟畔) is a Chinese transcription of a Yi (Wu-man) tribal and territorial name centered on modern Dongchuan/Huize during the Dali Kingdom.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a), recording Tanglang County in the Dongchuan/Huize region under Jianwei Commandery (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Dongchuan/Huize area was Tanglang County in the Han dynasty before becoming the seat of the Bipan (Mipan) tribe under the Dali Kingdom.

b_lulu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tang-era records Manshu (863 CE) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222b) as the Lulu Man (卢鹿蛮 / 盧鹿蠻), one of the seven Dongcuan Wu-man tribes allied with Nanzhao.
b_lulu.etymology_analysis: Lulu (卢鹿) is a Tang-era Chinese transcription of an indigenous Wu-man (proto-Yi) tribal name meaning 'tiger' (cognate with later Luoluo), located in northeastern Yunnan.

b_yilong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yilong County in 1289 CE (26th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan dynasty), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) as a former Dali-era Luowu tribal stronghold.
b_yilong.etymology_analysis: Per Yuanshi (Vol. 61), Yilong (易笼) derives from the local Wu-man words yi ('water', referring to two local streams) and long ('walled town').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), noting the Wuding/Luquan area belonged to Yaozhou in Tang times
older_name_by_867.notes: Under the Tang dynasty the area fell under Yaozhou jurisdiction before the Dali-era Luowu tribe built Yilong City.

b_nongdong.first_mention_attestation: Established in 109 BCE (2nd year of Yuanfeng, Western Han) as Nongdong County under Yizhou Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a), and later Nanzhao's Nongdong City in Manshu (Vol. 6).

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Yao'an basin

b_nongdong.etymology_analysis: Nongdong (弄栋) is a Han-era Chinese transcription of an indigenous Tibeto-Burman toponym in the Yao'an basin of northern Yunnan.

b_shenli.first_mention_attestation: Established in 637 CE (11th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Shenli County, seat of Weizhou jimi prefecture under Yaozhou Commandery (Xin Tangshu, Vol. 43b).
b_shenli.etymology_analysis: Shenli (深利) is a Tang-era administrative county name (modern Yongren County) serving as the seat of Weizhou jimi prefecture.

b_elu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) for the Tang/Nanzhao period (c. 750 CE), noting that Nanzhao's Geluofeng invaded Elu (俄碌) and captured Hezi City.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Chuxiong basin

b_elu.etymology_analysis: Elu (俄碌) is the indigenous Yi/Cuan name for the Chuxiong (Weichu) basin, attested in accounts of Nanzhao's 8th-century campaigns.

b_moyu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 or standard dynastic attestation found for Moyu (磨豫) in the Weichu/Chuxiong area.
b_moyu.etymology_analysis: Moyu (磨豫) lacks documented pre-867 attestation in Tang or Yuan historical geographies of Weichu.

b_huichuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huichuan Dudufu (会川都督府) by Nanzhao at the end of the Tianbao era (c. 754 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222a) and Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_huichuan_1.etymology_analysis: Huichuan (会川, 'converging valleys/assembly plain') was named in Tang/Nanzhao times as the strategic meeting point of regional chieftains and river valleys in southern Sichuan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a), recording Huiwu County under Yuexi Commandery (111 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Huiwu County was renamed Huichuan County in the Tang dynasty before falling to Nanzhao.

b_nuodan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (Vol. 2, 863 CE) as Nuodan (诺赕) under Huizhou/Huichuan, where the river from Taideng Mountain meets the East Lu River.
b_nuodan.etymology_analysis: Nuodan (诺赕) combines the local river/tribal name Nuo with the Nanzhao administrative term dan ('basin/district').

b_xituo.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) under Huili Prefecture as the Tang/Nanzhao-era local name Xituo (昔陀) under Huichuan Jiedu.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Huili area

b_xituo.etymology_analysis: Xituo (昔陀) is a Chinese transcription of the indigenous Tang/Nanzhao-era name for the Huili area southeast of Huichuan.

b_yuexi.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han) as Yuexi Commandery (越巂郡), recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a), and later Tang Yuexi County under Xizhou.
b_yuexi.etymology_analysis: Yuexi / Yuesui (越嶲) literally means 'crossing the Sui River,' referring to Han expansion across the Sui River (modern Anning River) into southwestern Sichuan.

b_taideng.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (Western Han) as Taideng County under Yuexi Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a), and served as the seat of Tang Xizhou from 832 CE.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Mianning valley

b_taideng.etymology_analysis: Taideng (台登) is a Han-era Chinese transcription of an indigenous Tibeto-Burman toponym in the Anning River valley (modern Mianning County).

b_chengji_1.first_mention_attestation: Opened by Nanzhao ruler Yimouxun in the Zhenyuan era (785–805 CE, c. 794 CE) and named Chengji Shan (成偈赕), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) and Mingshi (Vol. 314).

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Yongsheng basin

b_chengji_1.etymology_analysis: Chengji (成偈) is a Nanzhao-era transcription of an indigenous Bai/Loloish toponym for the Beisheng (modern Yongsheng) basin.

b_luogong.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) under Langqu Prefecture (蒗蕖州), which governed Luogong Shan (罗共赕) after its submission to the Yuan in 1272 CE.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Langqu basin

b_luogong.etymology_analysis: Luogong (罗共) is a Yuan-era transcription of a Mosuo/Yi toponym in the Ninglang/Langqu area.

b_songwai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Zizhi Tongjian (Zhenguan 22–23, 648–649 CE) as Songwai Man (松外蛮) and in Manshu (Vol. 6, 863 CE) as Songwai City (松外城).
b_songwai.etymology_analysis: Songwai (松外) is a Tang-era Chinese exonym/toponym meaning 'beyond the pines,' referring to a fortified Nanzhao/Mosuo settlement near the Jinsha River.

b_jianchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jianchuan Jiedu (剑川节度) by Nanzhao in the Zhenyuan era (c. 794 CE) after defeating the Langqiong Zhao, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222a) and Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_jianchuan.etymology_analysis: Jianchuan (剑川) is a Nanzhao-era toponym for the Jianchuan valley west of Jianhu Lake, later used for Jianchuan Jiedu and Jianchuan County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), noting Jianchuan's indigenous name was Luolucheng
older_name_by_867.notes: Before Nanzhao's Jianchuan Jiedu, the settlement was known locally as Luolucheng.

b_lanxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lanxi Commandery (兰溪郡) by the Duan family during the Dali Kingdom (937–1253 CE), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_lanxi.etymology_analysis: Lanxi (兰溪, noted in Yuanshi textual criticism as a variant of Lancang) derives from the nearby Lancang River and was established under the Dali Kingdom.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61) and Hou Hanshu, recording Han Bonan County (69 CE) and Tang Lulu Manbu
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Bonan County in 69 CE (Eastern Han) and known as the Lulu Man tribe in the Tang dynasty prior to the Dali Kingdom's Lanxi Commandery.

b_yunlong.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as Yunlong Dian Military and Civilian Prefecture (云龙甸军民府) in Yuanshi (Vol. 61, compiled 1370 CE), named for the morning clouds rising like a dragon over the Lancang River.
b_yunlong.etymology_analysis: Yunlong (云龙, 'cloud dragon') is a Yuan-era Chinese poetic name describing morning mists rising like a dragon over the Lancang River.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a), recording Bisu County under Yizhou Commandery (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: In the Han dynasty the Yunlong area was part of Bisu County.

b_kunmimg.first_mention_attestation: Established in 619 CE (2nd year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Kunming County under Xizhou (modern Yanyuan County, Sichuan), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) and Manshu (Vol. 6).
b_kunmimg.etymology_analysis: Kunming County (modern Yanyuan, Sichuan) was named after the ancient Kunming people (昆明夷) recorded since the Han dynasty.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Yuanshi (Vol. 61), recording Han Dingzuo County under Yuexi Commandery (111 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Han Dingzuo County (111 BCE) before Tang established Kunming County in 619 CE.

b_lidou.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) as Lidou Jiele (利窦揭勒), the indigenous name of Jin County/Jinzhou established in 1278 CE (15th year of Zhiyuan).
b_lidou.etymology_analysis: Lidou (利窦) is an abbreviation of Lidou Jiele (利窦揭勒), the Yuan-era transcription of the indigenous name for Jin County north of Yanyuan.

names: Northern border of Yuexi Commandery (越嶲郡北境)
older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), noting the area was the northern border of Han Yuexi Commandery (111 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Lay on the northern border of Han Yuexi Commandery before Yuan Zhiyuan 15 (1278 CE) established Jinzhou.

b_loutou.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) under Yongning Prefecture, formerly Loutou Shan (楼头赕) and locally named Dalan (答蓝), which submitted to the Mongols in 1253 CE.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Yongning basin

b_loutou.etymology_analysis: Dalan (答蓝) is the Mosuo/Naxi indigenous name for Loutou Shan (modern Yongning in Ninglang County), first documented in Yuan-era records.

b_muze.first_mention_attestation: Established as Muze Chiliarchy (目则千户) in 1257 CE (7th year of Xianzong, Mongol Empire), named after Mount Muze (目则山), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_muze.etymology_analysis: Muze (目则) is the indigenous name of Mount Muze (modern Mengzi), which was later phonetically corrupted in Chinese to Mengzi (蒙自).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a), recording Bengu County under Yizhou Commandery (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Bengu County was located in the modern Mengzi area.

b_ayue.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 or standard dynastic attestation found for Ayue (阿月) in the Mengzi/Muze area.
b_ayue.etymology_analysis: Ayue (阿月) appears to be a Yi/Tibeto-Burman-style toponym without documented pre-867 attestation in historical geographies.

b_mengpeng.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 or standard dynastic attestation found for Mengpeng (蒙彭) in the Mengzi/Muze area.
b_mengpeng.etymology_analysis: Mengpeng (蒙彭) lacks documented pre-867 attestation in Tang or Yuan historical geographies.

b_tonghai.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tonghai Dudufu (通海都督府) by Nanzhao in the late 8th century (c. 794 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222a) and Manshu (Vol. 6).
b_tonghai.etymology_analysis: Tonghai (通海, 'open to the lake/sea') was named by Nanzhao for its strategic position beside Qilu Lake on the route toward Annan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Manshu (Vol. 6), noting Tonghai occupied the former site of Han Yuyuan County (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Yuyuan County in 109 BCE before becoming Nanzhao's Tonghai Town / Commandery.

b_xie.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xi'e Prefecture (嶍峨州) in 1276 CE (13th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan dynasty), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).

natural_proper_name.name: Mount Xi and Mount E (嶍山、峨山)

b_xie.etymology_analysis: Xi'e (嶍峨, modern Eshan) derives from Mount Xi (associated with the Xi'ni tribe) and Mount E, first organized as an administrative unit in 1276 CE.

b_qixi.first_mention_attestation: First named Shiping Yi (石坪邑) in 752 CE (11th year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) under Tonghai Commandery, recorded in Shiping gazetteers and Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_qixi.etymology_analysis: Shiping (石坪, 'stone terrace', later altered to 石屏 in the Ming dynasty) describes the rocky plateau on which the settlement was built in 752 CE.

b_jianshui.first_mention_attestation: Built by Nanzhao in the Yuanhe era (c. 810 CE) as Huili City (惠𠠝城), rendered in Chinese as Jianshui (建水), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_jianshui.etymology_analysis: Jianshui (建水) is the Chinese translation/rendering of Nanzhao's Huili (惠𠠝, 'great water/sea'), built c. 810 CE on the earlier site of Butou/Badian.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61) and Manshu (Vol. 6), recording Butou and Badian as earlier names before Nanzhao built Huili/Jianshui c. 810 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Butou and Badian prior to Nanzhao's construction of Huili/Jianshui in the Yuanhe era (c. 810 CE).

b_hami_2.first_mention_attestation: Ami (阿迷, rendered here as Hami 哈迷) was established as Ami Chiliarchy/Prefecture in 1276 CE (13th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan dynasty), modern Kaiyuan.

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the Kaiyuan basin

b_hami_2.etymology_analysis: Hami (哈迷) represents Ami (阿迷), a Yuan-era Chinese transcription of an indigenous Yi toponym in the Kaiyuan basin.

b_baogu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Yuan records as the Huimo tribe (惠么部), which was reorganized into Weimo Prefecture (维摩州) in 1300 CE (4th year of Dade).

morphemes.translation: tribal ethnonym of the Huimo / Weimo

b_baogu.etymology_analysis: Huimo (惠么) is a Yuan-era transcription of the indigenous tribal name later standardized as Weimo (维摩) in southeastern Yunnan.

b_mile.first_mention_attestation: Established as Mile Chiliarchy in 1275 CE (12th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan dynasty) from the Mile tribe (弥勒部), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_mile.etymology_analysis: Mile (弥勒) is a Chinese transcription of the Ximotu/Yi tribal name Mile, which rose to prominence after the Tang era.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), noting the Guangxi Route area was inhabited by the Milu (弥鹿) and other Dongcuan Wu-man tribes in Tang times
older_name_by_867.notes: Inhabited by the Milu tribe under Tang jimi prefectures before the Mile tribe rose to prominence.

b_tuodong.first_mention_attestation: Built in 764 CE (2nd year of Guangde) by Nanzhao's Fengjiayi as Tuodong/Zhedong City (柘东城 / 拓东城), recorded in Manshu (Vol. 6) and Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_tuodong.etymology_analysis: Tuodong (拓东, also written 柘东) means 'expanding eastward,' reflecting Nanzhao's eastern capital built at modern Kunming in 764 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Manshu (Vol. 6), recording Han Guchang County (109 BCE) and Tang Kunzhou
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Han Guchang County and Sui-Tang Kunzhou before Fengjiayi built Tuodong City in 764 CE.

b_anning.first_mention_attestation: Established as Anning County under Kunzhou in the early Tang dynasty (c. 621 CE), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) and Manshu (Vol. 6).
b_anning.etymology_analysis: Anning (安宁, 'peace and tranquility') is an auspicious Tang-era Chinese administrative name given to the former Han Lianran County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Manshu (Vol. 6), noting Anning occupied the former site of Han Lianran County (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Lianran County (109 BCE) was renamed Anning County in the early Tang dynasty.

b_que.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (Vol. 6, 863 CE) as Qu'echuan (曲轭川), identified as the former Han/Jin Tongqi County.
b_que.etymology_analysis: Qu'e (曲轭, 'winding yoke') is a Tang-era Chinese river-valley name (Qu'echuan) recorded in Manshu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Manshu (Vol. 6), identifying Qu'echuan as the former Han/Jin Tongqi County
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Tongqi County in Han/Jin times before being recorded as Qu'echuan in Tang Manshu.

b_shicheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shicheng Commandery (石城郡) by Nanzhao at the end of the Tianbao era (c. 754 CE) after capturing Nanningzhou, recorded in Manshu (Vol. 6) and Yuanshi (Vol. 61).
b_shicheng_1.etymology_analysis: Shicheng (石城, 'stone citadel') was the Nanzhao-era name for the fortified seat at modern Qujing.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Manshu (Vol. 6), recording Han Wei County (109 BCE) and Tang Nanningzhou
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Han Wei County (109 BCE), later Liang/Tang Nanningzhou, renamed Shicheng by Nanzhao c. 754 CE.

b_yushi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yushi Myriarchy (于失万户) in 1257 CE (7th year of Xianzong, Mongol Empire) from the Yushi tribe (于矢部 / 于失部), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).

morphemes.translation: tribal ethnonym of the Yushi tribe

b_yushi.etymology_analysis: Yushi (于矢, also written 于失) is a Dali/Yuan-era transcription of an indigenous Cuan/Yi tribal name in the Pu'an region.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), recording Tang Xipingzhou and Panzhou before the rise of the Yushi tribe
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Xipingzhou and Panzhou in the early Tang dynasty.

b_shizong.first_mention_attestation: Submitted to the Mongols in 1257 CE (7th year of Xianzong) as the Shizong tribe (师宗部), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) as rising to prominence after the Tang era.
b_shizong.etymology_analysis: Shizong (师宗) is a Dali/Yuan-era Chinese transcription of a Cuan/Yi tribal name in southeastern Yunnan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanshi (Vol. 61), noting the area was inhabited by the Milu and other Dongcuan Wu-man tribes under Tang jimi prefectures
older_name_by_867.notes: Inhabited by the Milu tribe under Tang jimi prefectures before the Shizong tribe rose to prominence.

b_buri_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Buri Jian (步日睑) by Nanzhao under Yinsheng Jiedu (established 765 CE), recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61).

morphemes.translation: exonym for the Bulang ('my brother', Wa Paaex)

b_buri_2.etymology_analysis: Buri (步日) is a Nanzhao-era transcription of an Austroasiatic (Wa) ethnonym/toponym that later evolved into the name Pu'er (普洱).

b_buteng.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61) as one of the twelve tribes (including Buteng 步腾) incorporated into Yuanjiang Route in 1288 CE (25th year of Zhiyuan).
b_buteng.etymology_analysis: Buteng (步腾) is a Yuan-era Chinese transcription of an indigenous tribal name in southern Yunnan.

b_fengyi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (Vol. 6, 863 CE) as Fengyi City (奉逸城), governed by Kainan City under Nanzhao's Yinsheng Jiedu.
b_fengyi.etymology_analysis: Fengyi (奉逸) is a Nanzhao-era Chinese garrison/city name in southern Yunnan under Kainan City.

b_weiyuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (Vol. 6, 863 CE) as Weiyuan City (威远城), governed by Kainan City under Nanzhao's Yinsheng Jiedu.
b_weiyuan_1.etymology_analysis: Weiyuan (威远, 'awing the distant frontier') is a Nanzhao-era Chinese garrison/city name in modern Jinggu County.

b_luotuo.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for a settlement named Luotuo (罗罗陀 / Loluotuo) in the Weiyuan/Jinggu area of Yunnan; likely a later Yi/Lolo-period or game-derived toponym.

morphemes.translation: Lolo (historical Chinese exonym for Yi peoples)

b_luotuo.etymology_analysis: Luotuo (罗罗陀) appears to be a Chinese phonetic transcription combining the historical ethnonym Lolo (罗罗) with a topographic or phonetic suffix -tuo (陀). It is unattested in Tang/Nanzhao sources such as the Manshu (863 CE), which instead record Weiyuancheng (威远城) in this basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Manshu (蛮书), Vol. 6 (863 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Nanzhao garrison city Weiyuancheng (modern Weiyuan Town, Jinggu County) is attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (863 CE) under Kainan/Yinsheng.

b_menggu.first_mention_attestation: Attested only in post-867 CE Ming–Qing Dai tusi records (as a sub-polity/dowry territory of Mengwo/Jinggu); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_menggu.etymology_analysis: Menggu (勐谷) is a Southwestern Tai-derived toponym beginning with möng (勐, 'basin/polity') combined with gu (谷), documented in Ming–Qing Dai tusi records of the Jinggu/Yuanjiang region. In the Tang/Nanzhao period (<= 867 CE), the region was administered under Yinshengcheng and Kainancheng.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 222) and Manshu (863 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Nanzhao established the Yinsheng Jiedu (银生节度) and Kainancheng in 794 CE in the Jingdong/Pu'er region.

b_kainan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 794 CE (Tang Zhenyuan 10th year) as Kainancheng / Kainan Jiedu under Nanzhao, and recorded in Fan Chuo's Manshu (863 CE, Vol. 6) and Xin Tangshu.
b_kainan.etymology_analysis: Kainan (开南, 'opening the south') was a Nanzhao administrative and military commandery name established in the late 8th century (794 CE) in modern Jingdong Yi Autonomous County, Yunnan.

b_hepu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Fan Chuo's Manshu (蛮书, Vol. 6, 863 CE) as Hepuchuan (河普川), a river valley south of Yinshengcheng.
b_hepu.etymology_analysis: Hepu (河普) derives from Hepuchuan (河普川), a Tang-era Nanzhao river valley name recorded in the Manshu (863 CE) south of Yinshengcheng (identified with modern Jiangcheng, Yunnan).

b_puan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 554 CE (Western Wei Feidi 3rd year) as Pu'an County and Pu'an Commandery under Shizhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Taiping Huanyuji (Vol. 84).
b_puan.etymology_analysis: Pu'an (普安, 'universal peace') is an auspicious administrative name bestowed by Western Wei in 554 CE upon conquering Liang-held Anzhou (modern Jiange County, Sichuan).

b_jianmen.first_mention_attestation: Jianmen County (剑门县) was established in 699 CE (Wu Zhou Shengli 2nd year) under Shizhou (later Jianzhou), recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Taiping Huanyuji (Vol. 84); Jianmen Pass itself dates to the Three Kingdoms period.
b_jianmen.etymology_analysis: Jianmen (剑门, 'Sword Gate') is named after the strategic Jianmen Pass built between the cliff walls of Mount Dajian (大剑山) in northern Sichuan, which became the seat of Jianmen County in 699 CE.

b_zitong.first_mention_attestation: Established in 285 BCE (Qin King Zhaoxiang 22nd year) as Zitong County under Shu Commandery, attested in Liye Qin slips and Hanshu (Vol. 28a).
b_zitong.etymology_analysis: Zitong (梓潼) takes its name from its geographic setting—'backing on the Zilin (catalpa) forest to the east and bordering the Tong River (潼水) to the west,' as recorded in Huayang Guozhi.

b_jiangyou.first_mention_attestation: Established in 505 CE (Northern Wei Zhengshi 2nd year) as Jiangyou County (following the Three Kingdoms garrison Jiangyoushu), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29).

morphemes.translation: oil (clear/smooth like oil, or Youxi stream)

b_jiangyou.etymology_analysis: Jiangyou (江油) was named either for the Fu River's water being 'as clear and smooth as oil' or after the nearby Youxi (油溪) stream when Northern Wei founded Jiangyou County in 505 CE.

b_qingchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year) when Mapan County (马盘县) under Longzhou was renamed Qingchuan County, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_qingchuan.etymology_analysis: Qingchuan (清川, 'Clear Stream') was the Tang-era auspicious/descriptive county name given to Mapan County in 742 CE under Longzhou (Jiangyou Commandery) in northern Sichuan.

b_baxi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Baxi County (巴西县) in 581 CE (Sui Kaihuang 1st year) from Bazhong County (formerly Han Fu County), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_baxi.etymology_analysis: Baxi (巴西, 'West of Ba') was named in 581 CE because the county seat (modern Mianyang, Sichuan) had served as the seat of Baxi Commandery (established in the Eastern Han).

b_weicheng.first_mention_attestation: Established in 553 CE (Western Wei Feidi 2nd year) as Weicheng County split from Fu County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_weicheng.etymology_analysis: Weicheng (魏城, 'Wei City') was named after the Western Wei dynasty, which founded the county in 553 CE during its conquest of Sichuan.

b_anyue.first_mention_attestation: Established in 575 CE (Northern Zhou Jiande 4th year) as Anyue County alongside Puzhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_anyue.etymology_analysis: Anyue (安岳, 'peaceful dwelling upon the mountain') was founded by Northern Zhou in 575 CE as the seat of Puzhou, named for its hilltop strategic position.

b_anju.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Anju County in 593–598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 13th/18th year) from Rougang County (established 575 CE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_anju.etymology_analysis: Anju (安居, 'peaceful dwelling') was named by Sui in the 590s after the local Anju River (安居水) and Northern Zhou's Anju Commandery.

b_qi_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in the Western Han dynasty (c. 201 BCE) as Qi County (郪县) under Guanghan Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_qi_1.etymology_analysis: Qi (郪) is an ancient Sichuan county name (modern Santai County) attested from the Western Han, named after the Qi River (郪江).

b_yanting.first_mention_attestation: Established in 554 CE (Western Wei Gongdi 1st year; also attributed to Liang) as Yanting County on the site of earlier Chanting County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_yanting.etymology_analysis: Yanting (盐亭, 'Salt Pavilion/Post') takes its name from the salt wells and brine production in the area, which had earlier been called Chanting.

b_tongquan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tongquan County (renamed from Western Wei's Yongquan County) in the Sui Kaihuang era (581–600 CE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_tongquan.etymology_analysis: Tongquan (通泉, 'connecting springs') was a Sui-era county under Zizhou (Xincheng Commandery) in modern Shehong, Sichuan.

b_tongshan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 679 CE (Tang Tiaolu 1st year) as Tongshan County split from Qi and Feiwu counties under Zizhou, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_tongshan.etymology_analysis: Tongshan (铜山, 'Copper Mountain') was named after local copper-bearing mountains (in modern Zhongjiang County, Sichuan) when established by the Tang court in 679 CE.

b_panshi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Panshi County (盘石县) in 565 CE (Northern Zhou Baoding 5th year) from Han-era Zizhong County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_panshi.etymology_analysis: Panshi (盘石, 'Broad/Coiling Stone') was the Northern Zhou through Song name for modern Zizhong County, Sichuan, serving as the seat of Zizhou.

b_ziyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 560 CE (Northern Zhou Wucheng 2nd year) as Ziyang County on the site of ancient Zizhong, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).

morphemes.translation: north bank of a river / sunny side

b_ziyang.etymology_analysis: Ziyang (资阳) means 'on the yang (north) bank of the Zi River' (资水, modern Tuo River), as explained in Jiu Tangshu.

b_jingnan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 758 CE (Tang Qianyuan 1st year) as Jingnan County under Changzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi.
b_jingnan.etymology_analysis: Jingnan (静南, 'Pacifying the South') was a Tang administrative county created in 758 CE (and later seat of Changzhou in 775 CE) in modern Dazu, Chongqing.

b_yongchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 776 CE (Tang Dali 11th year) as Yongchuan County under Changzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_yongchuan.etymology_analysis: Yongchuan (永川) was named in 776 CE because three rivers converged in the town in the shape of the seal-script character 永 (yŏng).

b_luchuan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Luchuan County (泸川县) from Han-era Jiangyang County in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3rd year; Luzhou itself was established in Liang Datong 535–546 CE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_luchuan.etymology_analysis: Luchuan (泸川) was the Sui–Yuan county name for Luzhou (modern Luzhou, Sichuan), formed from the regional name Lu (泸) and chuan (川, 'river').

b_mianshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Mianshui County (绵水县) in the Liang dynasty (502–557 CE; or Jin per Jiu Tangshu) under Luzhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_mianshui.etymology_analysis: Mianshui (绵水) was a Liang–Tang county under Luzhou (modern Naxi District, Luzhou, Sichuan), named after the Mian River (绵水).

b_hejiang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 564 CE (Northern Zhou Baoding 4th year) when Anle Garrison (安乐戍) was converted into Hejiang County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_hejiang.etymology_analysis: Hejiang (合江, 'Confluence of Rivers') was named in 564 CE for its location at the confluence of the Chishui River and the Yangtze River.

b_bodao.first_mention_attestation: Walled in 182 BCE (Western Han Empress Lü 6th year; initially a Qin/Han 'dao' circuit for the Bo people), recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a) and Shiji.
b_bodao.etymology_analysis: Bodao (僰道) was the Qin–Tang administrative name for modern Yibin at the confluence of the Min and Jinsha rivers, designating a Han frontier district (-dao) among the Bo (僰) people.

b_yibin.first_mention_attestation: Established in the early Tang dynasty (Wude era, c. 618–626 CE) when Yu'e County (𨚲䣕县) under Rongzhou was renamed Yibin County (义宾县), recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41); later altered to 宜宾 in 977 CE.
b_yibin.etymology_analysis: Yibin (义宾, 'righteous submission/guest') was a Tang-era county name under Rongzhou (modern Yibin, Sichuan), renamed in 977 CE to 宜宾 to avoid Song Taizong Zhao Guangyi's naming taboo.

b_xuchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 627 CE (Tang Zhenguan 1st year) as Xuchuan County under Rongzhou (becoming seat of Rongzhou in 651 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_xuchuan.etymology_analysis: Xuchuan (旭川, 'Rising-Sun Stream') was a Tang-era county founded in 627 CE in modern Rong County, Sichuan, serving as the seat of Rongzhou from 651 CE.

b_gongjing.first_mention_attestation: Established in 618 CE (Tang Wude 1st year) as Gongjing County (seat of newly created Rongzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_gongjing.etymology_analysis: Gongjing (公井, 'Duke's/Public Well') was named after its ancient salt wells in modern Gongjing District, Zigong, Sichuan, becoming a county in 618 CE.

b_fangyi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fangyi County (方义县) from Xiaoxi County during Western Wei (c. 553–556 CE), becoming seat of Suizhou in 557 CE, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_fangyi.etymology_analysis: Fangyi (方义, 'upright righteousness') was the Western Wei through Five Dynasties name of the seat of Suizhou (modern Suining, Sichuan), before Song reverted it to Xiaoxi.

b_suining_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 347 CE (Eastern Jin Yonghe 3rd year) as Suining Commandery (遂宁郡), and in 707 CE (Tang Jinglong 1st year) as Suining County, recorded in Jinshu and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_suining_1.etymology_analysis: Suining (遂宁, 'achieving peace and tranquility') was bestowed by Huan Wen in 347 CE upon pacifying Cheng-Han in Sichuan.

b_shijing.first_mention_attestation: Established in 556 CE (Western Wei Gongdi 3rd year) as Shijing County (seat of Hezhou), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_shijing.etymology_analysis: Shijing (石镜, 'Stone Mirror') was named after a smooth, mirror-like rock outcrop along the Jialing/Fu confluence in modern Hechuan District, Chongqing.

b_ba.first_mention_attestation: Ancient state of Ba; Qin established Ba Commandery (巴郡) in 314 BCE, and Northern Zhou established Ba County (巴县) in 561 CE, recorded in Shiji and Suishu (Vol. 29).
b_ba.etymology_analysis: Ba (巴) preserves the ancient choronym of the pre-Qin State of Ba and Qin-era Ba Commandery, revived as Ba County in 561 CE (modern central Chongqing).

b_bishan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2nd year) as Bishan County (壁山县) under Yuzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Taiping Huanyuji.
b_bishan.etymology_analysis: Bishan (壁山, later written 璧山) was named in 757 CE after Chongbi Mountain (重壁山), whose cliffs rise like twin walls.

b_jiangjin.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jiangjin County (江津县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18th year) from Jiangyang County under Yuzhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Taiping Huanyuji (Vol. 136).
b_jiangjin.etymology_analysis: Jiangjin (江津, 'Yangtze River Ford') was named in 598 CE because the county seat sat at a major crossing/ferry point on the Yangtze River.

b_fuling.first_mention_attestation: Established in 140 BCE (Western Han Jianyuan 1st year) as Fuling County under Ba Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28a).
b_fuling.etymology_analysis: Fuling (涪陵) is named after the Fu River (涪水, historical name for the lower Wu River) and the hills/royal Ba tombs along its banks.

b_lewen.first_mention_attestation: Established in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) as Lewen County (initially under Nanlinzhou, transferred to Fuzhou in 626 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi.
b_lewen.etymology_analysis: Lewen (乐温) was named after Mount Lewen (乐温山) in modern Changshou District, Chongqing, as recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi.

b_wulong.first_mention_attestation: Established in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) as Wulong County under Fuzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Taiping Huanyuji.
b_wulong.etymology_analysis: Wulong (武龙, later written 武隆) takes its name from Mount Wulong (武龙山) within its territory, as noted in Taiping Huanyuji.

b_binhua.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Binhua County (宾化县) in 712 CE (Tang Xiantian 1st year) from Longhua County (established 637 CE) to avoid Emperor Xuanzong Li Longji's naming taboo, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_binhua.etymology_analysis: Binhua (宾化, 'submitting to civilizing influence') was a 712 CE Tang taboo-avoidance renaming of Longhua County (modern Nanchuan District, Chongqing).

b_fengjie.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fengjie County (奉节县) in 649 CE (Tang Zhenguan 23rd year) from Renfu County as the seat of Kuizhou, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_fengjie.etymology_analysis: Fengjie (奉节, 'upholding integrity') was bestowed by Emperor Taizong of Tang in 649 CE in honor of Zhuge Liang's unyielding fidelity at Baidicheng (modern Fengjie County, Chongqing).

b_dachang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Dachang County (大昌县) in Northern Zhou (557–581 CE) from Taichang County (泰昌县) to avoid Yuwen Tai's naming taboo, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_dachang.etymology_analysis: Dachang (大昌, 'Great Prosperity') was a Northern Zhou taboo-avoidance renaming of Jin-era Taichang County (modern Dachang Town, Wushan County, Chongqing).

b_wushan_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wushan County (巫山县) in 583 CE (Sui Kaihuang 3rd year) from Qin-era Wu County (巫县, 277 BCE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_wushan_1.etymology_analysis: Wushan (巫山) is named after Mount Wu (巫山), famous for the Wu Gorge of the Three Gorges on the Yangtze River.

b_yunan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yun'an County (云安县) in Northern Zhou (557–581 CE) from Han-era Quren County (朐忍县), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_yunan.etymology_analysis: Yun'an (云安, 'Cloud Peace') was the Northern Zhou through Song/Yuan name for modern Yunyang County, Chongqing (renamed Yunyang in the Ming dynasty).

b_nanpu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Nanpu County (南浦县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18th year) from Wanchuan County as the seat of Nanzhou (later Wanzhou), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_nanpu.etymology_analysis: Nanpu (南浦, 'Southern Riverbank') was the Sui–Yuan county name for modern Wanzhou District, Chongqing, reviving an earlier Jin-era name.

b_wuning_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wuning County (武宁县) in 575 CE (Northern Zhou Jiande 4th year) from Yuanyang County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_wuning_1.etymology_analysis: Wuning (武宁, 'pacifying the region through martial prowess') was established by Northern Zhou in 575 CE (modern Wuling Town, Wanzhou District, Chongqing).

b_liangshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liangshan County (梁山县) in 553 CE (Western Wei Yuanqin 2nd year), named after Mount Gaoliang (高粱山).
b_liangshan.etymology_analysis: Named after nearby Mount Gaoliang (高粱山) when Western Wei founded Liangshan County in 553 CE; renamed Liangping in 1952.

b_lichuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lichuan County (利川县) in 1735 CE (Qing Yongzheng 13th year) under Shi'nan Prefecture.
b_lichuan.etymology_analysis: A Qing-era auspicious county name created in 1735 CE during the gaitu guiliu (改土归流) reforms in western Hubei.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou / Book of Sui
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE, the Lichuan area fell under Tang Shizhou (est. 574 CE) and Qingjiang County (est. 583 CE).

b_linjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Linjiang County (临江县) in 112 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 5th year) under Ba Commandery.
b_linjiang.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Han-era county name meaning 'overlooking the river' (the Yangtze); seat of Tang Zhongzhou.

b_dianjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dianjiang County (垫江县) at its modern site in 553 CE (Western Wei); distinct from the Han-era Dianjiang County at modern Hechuan.
b_dianjiang.etymology_analysis: Western Wei revived the ancient Ba/Han name Dianjiang ('low-lying/winding river') for a new county in Linzhou (later Zhongzhou) in 553 CE.

b_nanbin.modern_name: Nanbin (Longhe Town, Fengdu / Shizhu area, Chongqing)
b_nanbin.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanbin County (南宾县) in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) under Linzhou (later Zhongzhou).
b_nanbin.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name in Zhongzhou (which was itself temporarily renamed Nanbin Commandery in 742 CE).

b_zunyi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zunyi County (遵义县) in 639 CE (Tang Zhenguan 13th year) under Bozhou (播州), recorded in the New Book of Tang.
b_zunyi.etymology_analysis: Confucian political-moral toponym ('follow righteousness') coined by the Tang court in 639 CE for Bozhou.

b_daishui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Daishui County (带水县) under Bozhou (播州) in 639 CE (Tang Zhenguan 13th year) in the New Book of Tang.
b_daishui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Daishui ('Girdle River') in Tang Bozhou.

b_nanchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanchuan County (南川县) in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) as the seat of Nanzhou (南州).
b_nanchuan.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name ('Southern River') established in 619 CE; later merged with Longhua County in 1285 CE.

b_sanxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Sanxi County (三溪县) in 631 CE (Tang Zhenguan 5th year) under Nanzhou, named after the confluence of Boxi, Dongxi, and Gexi streams.
b_sanxi.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic county name referring to the confluence of three mountain streams (Boxi, Dongxi, and Gexi).

b_pengshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Pengshui County (彭水县) in 593 CE (Sui Kaihuang 13th year) as the seat of Qianzhou.
b_pengshui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Pengshui River (Peng River) when Sui established the county in 593 CE.

b_qianjiang_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qianjiang County (黔江县) in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year) under Qianzhou, previously Shicheng County.
b_qianjiang_1.etymology_analysis: Named after the Qianjiang River (Wujiang/Qian River) in 742 CE, replacing the earlier Sui name Shicheng.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Sui / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally established as Shicheng County in 585 CE (Sui Kaihuang 5th year) before being renamed Qianjiang in 742 CE.

b_duru.first_mention_attestation: Established as Duru County (都濡县) in 646 CE (Tang Zhenguan 20th year) under Qianzhou, split from Yinglong County.
b_duru.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Qianzhou established in 646 CE, likely transcribing a local non-Sinitic toponym with riverine semantics.

b_duhong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hongdu County (洪杜县) in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) under Qianzhou (keyed as b_duhong, hanzi 洪杜).
b_duhong.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Qianzhou founded in 619 CE; later became Hongdu Stockade (洪杜寨) in Song.

b_qingjiang_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qingjiang County (清江县) in early Sui (581–583 CE) from Shaqu County, serving as the seat of Shizhou (施州).
b_qingjiang_1.etymology_analysis: Named after the Qingjiang River ('Clear River') flowing through Enshi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou / Book of Sui
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Shaqu County in 574 CE (Northern Zhou Jiande 3rd year) and renamed Qingjiang County in Sui.

b_jianshi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jianshi County (建始县) in 574 CE (Northern Zhou Jiande 3rd year) as the seat of Yezhou (业州), later under Shizhou.
b_jianshi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('founding the beginning') given by Northern Zhou in 574 CE.

b_xisha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; Tang and Song Shizhou (清江郡) only recorded Qingjiang and Jianshi counties.
b_xisha.etymology_analysis: Descriptive local toponym ('Fine Sand') not attested as a pre-867 CE administrative seat or settlement.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou / Old Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: By 867 CE, the surrounding area was administered under Tang Shizhou (est. 574 CE) and Qingjiang County.

b_geluo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; no Tang or Song county or fortress of this name is recorded under Shizhou.
b_geluo.etymology_analysis: Local or tusi-era toponym (likely a phonetic transcription) unattested in Tang or earlier records.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou / Old Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: By 867 CE, the surrounding area was administered under Tang Shizhou and Jianshi County (both est. 574 CE).

b_wuchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuchuan County (务川县) in 599 CE (Sui Kaihuang 19th year), becoming the seat of Wuzhou/Sizhou.
b_wuchuan.etymology_analysis: Sui-era county name in northeastern Guizhou, seat of Tang Sizhou (思州).

b_siqiong.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Siqiong County (思邛县, abbreviated in-game as 邛) under Tang Sizhou in the Tianbao era (742 CE) in the New Book of Tang.
b_siqiong.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Sizhou (思州), combining the prefecture prefix Si- with the local river/toponym Qiong.

b_fuchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fuchuan County (涪川县) in 585 CE (Sui Kaihuang 5th year) under Qian'an Commandery, recorded in Yudi Guangji.
b_fuchuan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Fuchuan / Fu River (modern Wujiang tributary) in 585 CE; later part of Tang Sizhou and Feizhou.

b_ningyi.first_mention_attestation: Chengle County (城乐县, audited per b_hanzi 城乐) was established in the Tang Wude era (618–626 CE) under Sizhou; Ningyi County (宁夷县) was likewise established in 621 CE.
b_ningyi.etymology_analysis: Per Ming Yitongzhi, Chengle ('Joyful Citadel') was named during Tang Wude when locals sang and danced upon the building of its walls.

b_suiyang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Suiyang County (绥阳县) by 637 CE (Tang Zhenguan 11th year) when Tang Yizhou moved its seat to Suiyang (originally created in Sui Daye).
b_suiyang.etymology_analysis: Sui-Tang frontier county name ('pacifying the sunny/south side'), serving as the seat of Tang Yizhou (夷州).

b_yangchuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yangchuan County (洋川县) under Tang Yizhou (夷州) by the Tianbao era (742 CE) in the Old and New Books of Tang.
b_yangchuan.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Yizhou named after the local Yangchuan stream.

b_yiquan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yiquan County (义泉县) and Yiquan Commandery under Tang Yizhou (夷州) by 742 CE (Tianbao 1st year) in the Old and New Books of Tang.
b_yiquan.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Yizhou named after a local spring ('Righteous Spring').

b_rongyi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Rongyi County (荣懿县) in 642 CE (Tang Zhenguan 16th year) as the seat of Zhenzhou (溱州).
b_rongyi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era county name created in 642 CE for Zhenzhou (溱州).

b_leyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Leyuan County (乐源县) in 642 CE (Tang Zhenguan 16th year) under Zhenzhou (珍州).
b_leyuan.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Zhenzhou (珍州) established in 642 CE; Song Zhenzhou was also called Leyuan Commandery (乐源郡).

b_yelang.first_mention_attestation: Ancient polity of Yelang (夜郎) attested in Shiji (c. 135 BCE, Tang Meng's mission); Tang Yelang County (夜郎县) under Zhenzhou was established in 643 CE.
b_yelang.etymology_analysis: Han-era Chinese phonetic transcription of an indigenous southwestern ethnic/polity name, revived for a Tang county in 643 CE.

b_daxiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Daxiang County (大乡县) in 691 CE (Wu Zhou Tianshou 2nd year) as the seat of Xizhou (溪州 / Lingxi Commandery).
b_daxiang.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name ('Great Township') established in 691 CE as the administrative center of Xizhou.

b_danting.first_mention_attestation: Established as Santing County (三亭县, keyed b_danting, hanzi 三亭) in 691 CE (Wu Zhou Tianshou 2nd year) under Xizhou / Lingxi Commandery.
b_danting.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county in Xizhou ('Three Post Stations'), located along the Youshui river route in modern Longshan County.

b_huixi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 940 CE (Later Jin Tianfu 5th year) when Ma Xifan of Chu moved the seat of Xizhou to Huixicheng (会溪城) following the Xizhou Bronze Pillar treaty.
b_huixi.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic settlement name ('Converging Brook') that became the seat of Xizhou in 940 CE under Ma Chu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to 940 CE, Xizhou was seated at Daxiang County (est. 691 CE).

b_yuanling.first_mention_attestation: Established as the Marquisate/County of Yuanling (沅陵) in Western Han (187 BCE, Empress Lü 1st year, granted to Wu Yang).
b_yuanling.etymology_analysis: Named after the Yuan River (沅水) and surrounding hills (陵); seat of Chenzhou (辰州) from 589 CE.

b_chenxi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Chenxi County (辰溪县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9th year) from Han Chenyang County.
b_chenxi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chenxi ('Chen Brook', one of the Five Streams / 五溪) in 589 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally established as Chenyang County in Western Han before being renamed Chenxi in 589 CE.

b_xupu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xupu County (溆浦县) in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5th year) under Chenzhou on the former territory of Han Yiling County.
b_xupu.etymology_analysis: Named after the Xu River (溆水) and its banks when Tang founded the county in 622 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han
older_name_by_867.notes: Occupied the territory of Western Han Yiling County.

b_xuangu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the History of Song (Geographic Treatise) as Xuangu Stockade (悬鼓砦) under Xupu County, Chenzhou (Song Xining/Yuanfeng era, c. 1079 CE).
b_xuangu.etymology_analysis: Song-era military stockade (悬鼓砦) in Xupu County, Chenzhou, named after a drum-shaped peak or rock.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE, the area was part of Tang Xupu County (est. 622 CE) in Chenzhou.

b_chipeng.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; no Tang or earlier county or fortress of this name is recorded under Chenzhou.
b_chipeng.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name ('Sagebrush Pool') unattested in pre-867 CE historical records.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Sui / Old Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE, the area fell under Tang Chenzhou (est. 589 CE).

b_luyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Luyang County (卢阳县) in 686 CE (Tang Chuigong 2nd year) as the seat of Jinzhou (锦州 / Luyang Commandery).
b_luyang.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county founded in 686 CE as the seat of Jinzhou (note: distinct from the Southern Chen Luyang Commandery in Rucheng).

b_changfeng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Changfeng County (常丰县) in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year) from Wan'an County under Jinzhou.
b_changfeng.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang Tianbao-era renaming ('Enduring Abundance') of Wan'an County in 742 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally established as Wan'an County (万安县) in 686 CE under Jinzhou before being renamed Changfeng in 742 CE.

b_zhaoyu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhaoyu County (招谕县) under Tang Jinzhou (锦州, est. 686 CE), recorded in the Old and New Books of Tang.
b_zhaoyu.etymology_analysis: Tang frontier county name ('Summon and Instruct' the highland peoples) under Jinzhou.

b_shanxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shangxi Prefecture (上溪州) in the Five Dynasties (c. 940 CE) when Ma Chu divided Xizhou into Xiazhou, Shangxizhou, and Baojingzhou.
b_shanxi.etymology_analysis: Topographic/hydronymic name ('Upper Brook') created in the 10th century when Xizhou was partitioned under Ma Chu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE, the area was part of Tang Xizhou (est. 691 CE).

b_anfu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Anfu County (安福县) in 1729 CE (Qing Yongzheng 7th year) in Hunan; renamed Linli County in 1914.
b_anfu.etymology_analysis: Qing-era auspicious county name created in 1729 CE during the Yongzheng reforms.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: By 867 CE, the region fell under Tang Xizhou (est. 691 CE) and Lizhou.

b_baoshun.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Baojingzhou / Baoshunzhou (保静州 / 保顺州 in History of Song vol. 493), partitioned from Xizhou in the Five Dynasties (c. 940 CE).
b_baoshun.etymology_analysis: Five Dynasties / Song jimi prefecture name ('Protect and Submit') under the Peng tusi of Xizhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE, the area was part of Tang Xizhou (est. 691 CE).

b_longbiao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Longbiao County (龙标县) in the Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE); later seat of Tang Wuzhou (est. 634 CE) and Xuzhou.
b_longbiao.etymology_analysis: Southern Dynasties county name made famous by Wang Changling's Tang exile poetry ('Drifting to Longbiao').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han / Book of Jin
older_name_by_867.notes: Succeeded Western Han Wuyang County (无阳) and Jin Wuyang County (舞阳).

b_tanyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tanyang County (潭阳县) in 713 CE (Tang Xiantian 2nd year), split from Longbiao County; also Tanyang Commandery (742 CE).
b_tanyang.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name in Wuzhou/Xuzhou established in 713 CE, predecessor of Qing Zhijiang County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han / Old Book of Tang
older_name_by_867.notes: Split from Longbiao County (502 CE), on territory of Han Wuyang County.

b_langxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Langxi County (朗溪县, also written 郎溪) in 634 CE (Tang Zhenguan 8th year) under Wuzhou (later Xuzhou).
b_langxi.etymology_analysis: Tang-era hydronymic county name in Wuzhou/Xuzhou founded in 634 CE.

b_tongdao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tongdao County (通道县) in 1103 CE (2nd year of Chongning, Northern Song dynasty), renamed from Luomeng County (罗蒙县, founded 1102 CE), as recorded in Songshi (Vol. 88).
b_tongdao.etymology_analysis: Tongdao (通道, 'open thoroughfare') was a Northern Song auspicious administrative name bestowed in 1103 CE, referring to the strategic mountain corridor linking Hunan, Guangxi, and Guizhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28) / Xin Tangshu (Vol. 41)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Qin and Han times the area belonged to Tancheng County (established 221 BCE under Xiang Commandery), and during the Tang dynasty it was part of Langxi and Tanyang counties under Wuzhou/Xuzhou.

b_eshan.first_mention_attestation: Named Eshan County (峨山县) in 732 CE (20th year of Kaiyuan, Tang dynasty) when Yelang County was renamed Eshan under Yezhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_eshan.etymology_analysis: Eshan (峨山, 'lofty mountain') is a Tang-era county name derived from the steep mountainous terrain of western Hunan (modern Xinhuang Dong Autonomous County).

b_zijiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zijiang County (梓姜县) by 744 CE (3rd year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty), when it was transferred from Chongzhou to Yezhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Jiu Tangshu.
b_zijiang.etymology_analysis: Zijiang (梓姜) is a Tang-era county name in eastern Guizhou (modern Shibing County), likely transcribing or sinicizing a local non-Han toponym using the characters for catalpa and Qiang.

b_weixi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Weixi County (渭溪县) in 691 CE (2nd year of Tianshou, Wu Zhou) by splitting Yelang County, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_weixi.etymology_analysis: Weixi (渭溪, 'Wei Brook') is a Tang-era county name in eastern Guizhou (modern Xindian Town, Yuping County) named after a local stream.

b_shian.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shi'an County (始安县) in 630 CE (4th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as one of five counties under Yanzhou (琰州), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_shian.etymology_analysis: Shi'an (始安, 'first pacification') is a Tang-era auspicious administrative name given to a subordinate county of Yanzhou in central Guizhou.

b_lainan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, or Qing geographical treatises; appears to be an unattested or corrupted in-game barony name under Luodian.
b_lainan.etymology_analysis: Lainan (来南, 'coming to the south') is not documented in historical Chinese gazetteers for Guizhou and likely represents a synthetic or corrupted game toponym.

b_yanchuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yanchuan County (琰川县) during the Zhenguan era (627–649 CE, Tang dynasty) under Yanzhou (琰州, founded 630 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_yanchuan_1.etymology_analysis: Yanchuan (琰川, 'Yan River/Valley') is a Tang-era jimi county name derived from Yanzhou (琰州) and its river valley in central Guizhou.

b_jiangzhou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiangzhou (姜州) in 663 CE (3rd year of Longshuo, Tang dynasty) by splitting Mingzhou under Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_jiangzhou.etymology_analysis: Jiangzhou (姜州) is a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command located in the Kaili area of southeastern Guizhou.

b_wuhou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuhou County (武侯县) in 630 CE (4th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) under Yanzhou (琰州), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_wuhou.etymology_analysis: Wuhou (武侯, 'Martial Marquis', an honorific associated with Zhuge Liang in southwest China) was a Tang-era subordinate county of Yanzhou.

b_jiangkun.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Longkun County (隆昆县, rendered 降昆 in-game) during the Zhenguan era (627–649 CE, Tang dynasty) under Yanzhou (琰州, founded 630 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).

morphemes.translation: to subdue / descend (variant of 隆 lóng)

b_jiangkun.etymology_analysis: Jiangkun (降昆) corresponds to the Tang-era Yanzhou subordinate county Longkun (隆昆县) recorded in Xin Tangshu, reflecting a graphic variant between 降 and 隆.

b_qinglan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qinglan County (清兰县) during the Zhenguan era (627–649 CE, Tang dynasty) under Zhuangzhou (庄州, renamed 630 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_qinglan.etymology_analysis: Qinglan (清兰, 'pure orchid') is a Tang-era jimi county name under Zhuangzhou in central Guizhou.

b_qingxi_2.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Qingxi Town (清溪镇) in late Tang (c. late 9th to early 10th century, '唐末') when Nanningzhou was re-established there, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b); later Qingxi County (青溪县) in Guizhou was established in 1727 CE.
b_qingxi_2.etymology_analysis: Qingxi (清溪, 'clear brook') refers to Qingxi Town attested at the end of the Tang dynasty (post-867 CE) and later Qingxi County in Zhenyuan, Guizhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28) / Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b)
older_name_by_867.notes: The region belonged to Zangke Commandery (founded 111 BCE) and Tang Nanningzhou (618 CE) prior to the late-Tang settlement at Qingxi Town.

b_xizhou.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Huizhou (晖州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_xizhou.etymology_analysis: Huizhou (晖州, 'radiant prefecture') is a Tang jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command located in the Zhijin–Nayong area of western Guizhou.

b_haozhou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haozhou (郝州, written 都州 in Xin Tangshu) in 663 CE (3rd year of Longshuo, Tang dynasty) under Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) and Yuanfeng Jiuyu Zhi.
b_haozhou.etymology_analysis: Haozhou (郝州) is a Tang jimi prefecture established in 663 CE for Wuman/Kunming tribes in the Dafang area of northwestern Guizhou.

b_gongzhou.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gongzhou (功州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_gongzhou.etymology_analysis: Gongzhou (功州, 'meritorious prefecture') is a Tang jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command in Guizhou.

b_puning.first_mention_attestation: Established as Puningzhou (普宁州) in 663 CE (3rd year of Longshuo, Tang dynasty) for Wuman/Kunming tribes under Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_puning.etymology_analysis: Puning (普宁, 'universal peace') is a Tang auspicious jimi prefecture name established in 663 CE under Qianzhou Area Command.

b_qushui_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qushui County (曲水县) in 690 CE (2nd year of Zaichu, Wu Zhou) as the seat of Shunzhou under Luzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_qushui_1.etymology_analysis: Qushui (曲水, 'winding river') is a Tang-era jimi county in northern Guizhou/southern Sichuan (modern Xishui County area) named after a meandering river.

b_humao.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Nazhou (纳州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Luzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_humao.etymology_analysis: Nazhou (纳州, 'tribute-receiving prefecture') is a Tang jimi prefecture under Luzhou Area Command in southern Sichuan (Luzhou–Jiang'an–Hejiang area).

b_zheyuan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, or Qing geographical treatises for Sichuan or Guizhou; appears to be an unattested in-game barony name.
b_zheyuan.etymology_analysis: Zheyuan (淅源, 'source of the Xi River') is not attested in historical southwest Chinese gazetteers under Shunzhou or Luzhou.

b_sie.first_mention_attestation: Established as Si'e County (思峨县) in 677 CE (2nd year of Yifeng, Tang dynasty) under Yanzhou, and elevated to Si'ezhou (思峨州) in 690–691 CE under Luzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_sie.etymology_analysis: Si'e (思峨) is a Tang-era jimi county and prefecture name under Luzhou Area Command in southern Sichuan.

b_yujing.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yujing Salt Superintendency (淯井监) in 1013 CE (6th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song dynasty) in Songshi (Vol. 496), located at modern Shuanghe Town, Changning County, Sichuan.
b_yujing.etymology_analysis: Yujing (淯井, 'Yu salt well') was a Northern Song salt-producing settlement and military superintendency in southern Sichuan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b)
older_name_by_867.notes: In 700 CE (1st year of Jiushi, Wu Zhou), the Tang established the jimi prefecture of Yuzhou (淯州) in this same southern Sichuan area.

b_fengzhou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fengzhou (奉州) in 677 CE (2nd year of Yifeng, Tang dynasty) as a jimi prefecture under Luzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_fengzhou.etymology_analysis: Fengzhou (奉州, 'reverent prefecture') is a Tang jimi prefecture established in 677 CE under Luzhou Area Command.

b_fude.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fudezhou (扶德州) and Fude County (扶德县), a Tang-era jimi prefecture/county under Rongzhou and Luzhou Area Commands (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_fude.etymology_analysis: Fude (扶德, 'upholding virtue') is a Tang auspicious jimi prefecture and county name in southern Sichuan.

b_songshui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Mangbu tribe (芒布部) in the Yuan dynasty (1276 CE / Zhiyuan 13th year) under Wusa Route, recorded in Yuanshi (Vol. 61), corresponding to modern Zhenxiong County, Yunnan.
b_songshui.etymology_analysis: Mangbu (芒布) is a Chinese transcription of a Wuman/Yi tribal name first attested in Yuan-era records for northeastern Yunnan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Han and Tang times the northeastern Yunnan region belonged to Zhuti (established 135 BCE) and Nanguang.

b_yanquan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yanquan County (盐泉县) in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) under Yinzhou in Rongzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_yanquan.etymology_analysis: Yanquan (盐泉, 'salt spring') is a Tang jimi county name under Yinzhou in Yunnan/Sichuan borderlands, named for local brine springs.

b_yanshui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bolingzhou (播陵州) and Boling County (播陵县), a Tang-era jimi prefecture/county split from Yingzhou under Rongzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_yanshui.etymology_analysis: Boling (播陵) is a Tang jimi prefecture and county name under Rongzhou Area Command in the Sichuan–Yunnan borderlands.

b_jingchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dong'an County (东安县) in 618 CE (1st year of Wude, Tang dynasty) under Xiezhou in Rongzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_jingchuan.etymology_analysis: Dong'an (东安, 'eastern peace') is a Tang jimi county under Xiezhou in northeastern Yunnan.

b_humu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fenxie County (分协县) by 625 CE (8th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) when Jingzhou was split from Xiezhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_humu.etymology_analysis: Fenxie (分协, 'branch of Xiezhou') is a Tang county name in modern Xuanwei, Yunnan, reflecting its administrative origin from Xiezhou.

b_xunlu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Shimen Pass (石门关) and the Shimen Route (石门道) in the 794 CE Yuan Zi cliff inscription (袁滋题记摩崖石刻) at Doushaguan, Yanjin County, Yunnan, and in Xin Tangshu.
b_xunlu.etymology_analysis: Shimen (石门, 'stone gate') refers to the narrow cliff gorge and strategic Tang-era pass on the route between Sichuan and Yunnan.

b_zhuti.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhuti County (朱提县) under Qianwei Commandery in 135 BCE (6th year of Jianyuan, Western Han dynasty), recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28); later seat of Tang Quzhou.
b_zhuti.etymology_analysis: Zhuti (朱提, traditionally glossed in Hanshu as pronounced Zhūshí) is a Han-era administrative name in northeastern Yunnan (modern Zhaotong), famous for its silver mines.

b_dongan_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dong'an County (东安县) in 618 CE (1st year of Wude, Tang dynasty) under Xiezhou in Rongzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_dongan_2.etymology_analysis: Dong'an (东安, 'eastern peace') is a Tang jimi county under Xiezhou in northeastern Yunnan.

b_yinzhou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yinzhou (殷州) in 672 CE (3rd year of Xianheng, Tang dynasty) from Kunming tribal territory, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_yinzhou.etymology_analysis: Yinzhou (殷州) is a Tang jimi prefecture established in 672 CE under Rongzhou Area Command (later transferred to Qianzhou Area Command).

b_kaibian.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kaibian County (开边县) by 607 CE (3rd year of Daye, Sui dynasty) under Qianwei Commandery, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_kaibian.etymology_analysis: Kaibian (开边, 'opening the frontier') is a Sui–Tang county name in southern Sichuan (modern Yibin/Anbian area) reflecting imperial frontier expansion.

b_muyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Muyuan Town (沐源镇) in 875 CE (2nd year of Qianfu, Tang dynasty) when a garrison fort was built against local Man/Yi incursions, recorded in local Muchuan gazetteers.
b_muyuan.etymology_analysis: Muyuan (沐源, 'source of the Mu River') was founded as a late-Tang garrison town in 875 CE, eight years after the 867 CE baseline, and later became Muchuan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Vol. 28)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Han times the area belonged to Qianwei Commandery (established 135 BCE) and was inhabited by the Bo people.

b_guile.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Guilezhou (归乐州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Yongzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_guile.etymology_analysis: Guile (归乐, 'returning to allegiance in joy') is a Tang auspicious jimi prefecture name under Yongzhou Area Command in Guangxi.

b_lengzhou.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lengzhou (稜州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_lengzhou.etymology_analysis: Lengzhou (稜州) is a Tang jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command recorded in Xin Tangshu.

b_shuangcheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shuangchengzhou (双城州) in 698 CE (1st year of Shengli, Wu Zhou) by splitting Lengzhou under Zhuangzhou/Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_shuangcheng.etymology_analysis: Shuangcheng (双城, 'twin citadels') is a Tang-era jimi prefecture established in 698 CE.

b_siyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Siyuanzhou (思源州) during 698–710 CE (Wu Zhou/Tang) by splitting Xuanzhou under Zhuangzhou/Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_siyuan.etymology_analysis: Siyuan (思源, 'remembering the source') is a Tang jimi prefecture name under Qianzhou Area Command.

b_temo.first_mention_attestation: Established as Temodao (特磨道) in 971 CE (4th year of Kaibao, Northern Song / Dali Kingdom) when Dali occupied former Southern Han jimi lands in southeastern Yunnan, recorded in Songshi (Vol. 495).
b_temo.etymology_analysis: Temo (特磨) is a Zhuang/Tai-derived toponym first attested in 971 CE as a Dali Kingdom frontier circuit (Temodao) in modern Funing and Guangnan, Yunnan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b)
older_name_by_867.notes: During the Tang dynasty, the Funing area was administered as the jimi prefecture of Dongjianzhou under Guizhou Area Command.

b_wulong_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wulong County (武龙县) in 619 CE (2nd year of Wude, Tang dynasty) in Fuling (modern Chongqing), and also attested as Wulong County in Guangxi in 627 CE (1st year of Zhenguan) under Yanzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu.
b_wulong_1.etymology_analysis: Wulong (武龙, 'martial dragon') is a Tang-era county name attested in both Guangxi (627 CE) and Chongqing (619 CE).

b_dongjian.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dongjianzhou (洞监州), a Tang-era jimi prefecture under Guizhou Area Command (7th–8th century CE), located at modern Boai Town, Funing County, Yunnan.
b_dongjian.etymology_analysis: Dongjian (洞监, 'valley-settlement superintendency') is a Tang jimi prefecture name in southeastern Yunnan.

b_sigang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Temodao (特磨道) in 971 CE (4th year of Kaibao, Northern Song / Dali Kingdom) in southeastern Yunnan, recorded in Songshi (Vol. 495).
b_sigang.etymology_analysis: Temo (特磨) is a Zhuang/Tai-derived toponym first attested in 971 CE as a Dali Kingdom frontier circuit (Temodao) in modern Funing and Guangnan, Yunnan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b)
older_name_by_867.notes: During the Tang dynasty, the Funing area was administered as the jimi prefecture of Dongjianzhou under Guizhou Area Command.

b_leshan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Leshanzhou (乐善州) in 1080 CE (Yuanfeng era, Northern Song) in Yuanfeng Jiuyu Zhi (Vol. 10) and Songshi (Vol. 89) as a jimi prefecture under Shaoqing Fu; not attested in Tang sources.
b_leshan.etymology_analysis: Leshan (乐善, 'delighting in goodness') is a Song-attested jimi prefecture name in the Guizhou–Guangxi borderlands.

b_lexing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lexing Commandery (乐兴郡) and Lexing County (乐兴县) in 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) when Guzhou was renamed Lexing Commandery in southeastern Guizhou.
b_lexing.etymology_analysis: Lexing (乐兴, 'joyful prosperity') is a Tang-era commandery and county name in the Congjiang–Rongjiang area of southeastern Guizhou.

b_gushu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 638 CE (12th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Gushu County under Guzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_gushu.etymology_analysis: Gushu (古书) was established as one of the three counties of Guzhou in 638 CE when Tang general Li Hongjie opened the Miao/Dong frontier in southeastern Guizhou (modern Rongjiang County).

b_bianxi.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1292 CE (29th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan dynasty) as Bianxi Water Station (便溪水站) along the Yuan–Wu river postal route from Yuezhou to Zhenyuan.
b_bianxi.etymology_analysis: Bianxi (便溪, 'convenient stream') is a Yuan-era water relay station name on the Wushui/Yuan River route near Huangzhou (modern Xinhuang, Hunan), later echoed by the Ming-era Bianshui Post.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) and Xinhuang County records: Yelang County was established in 634 CE (Zhenguan 8) and Huangzhou in 641 CE (Zhenguan 15).
older_name_by_867.notes: In the Tang dynasty, the Xinhuang/Huangzhou area was administered as Yelang County (634 CE) and Huangzhou jimi prefecture (641 CE).

b_tonggu_1.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1103 CE (2nd year of Chongning, Northern Song dynasty) when Tonggu Stockade (铜鼓寨) was established under Jingzhou.
b_tonggu_1.etymology_analysis: Tonggu (铜鼓, 'bronze drum') refers to the traditional bronze drums of the southwestern Dong and Miao peoples; the settlement was first fortified as Tonggu Stockade by the Northern Song in 1103 CE (modern Jinping County, Guizhou).

b_pingan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE historical attestation found for a settlement or administrative unit named Ping'an (平安) in the Juzhou (Guiyang) region of Guizhou.
b_pingan.etymology_analysis: Ping'an (平安) is an auspicious Chinese toponym meaning 'peace and tranquility,' unattested in Tang-era records for Juzhou (modern Guiyang area).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b), recording Juzhou established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty).
older_name_by_867.notes: The Guiyang basin was administered by the Tang as Juzhou (621 CE) and Zangzhou (620 CE).

b_binhua_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in early Kaihuang (c. 581 CE, Sui dynasty) as Binhua County under Zangzhou (Zangke Commandery), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).

morphemes.translation: guest / to submit as a tributary

b_binhua_1.etymology_analysis: Binhua (宾化, 'submitting to civilizing influence') is a Sui-dynasty frontier county name reflecting the imperial policy of integrating local Zangke chieftains in central Guizhou (modern Guiding area).

b_shiniu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 629 CE (3rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Shiniu County under Zhuangzhou (originally Nanshouzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_shiniu.etymology_analysis: Shiniu (石牛, 'stone ox') is a Tang-era county established in 629 CE under Zhuangzhou in central Guizhou, typically named after a prominent ox-shaped rock formation.

b_shicheng.first_mention_attestation: Established in 629 CE (3rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Shicheng County under Zhuangzhou (originally Nanshouzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_shicheng.etymology_analysis: Shicheng (石城, 'stone fortress') was established in 629 CE under Zhuangzhou in central Guizhou, referring to a stone-built stronghold or natural rocky citadel.

b_nanping.first_mention_attestation: Established in 630 CE (4th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Nanping County and seat of Nanpingzhou (later Bazhou, then under Yuzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_nanping.etymology_analysis: Nanping (南平, 'southern pacification') was created in 630 CE out of Ba County south of the Yangtze River (modern Banan/Qijiang area, Chongqing) as the seat of Nanpingzhou.

b_maolong.first_mention_attestation: Established in 698 CE (1st year of Shengli, Wu Zhou / Tang dynasty) as Maolongzhou (茂龙州), a jimi prefecture split from Laozhou under Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_maolong.etymology_analysis: Maolong (茂龙) is the name of a Tang jimi prefecture established in 698 CE under Qianzhou Area Command (modern southwestern Guizhou / Anlong area).

b_xunzhou.first_mention_attestation: Established in 655 CE (6th year of Yonghui, Tang dynasty) as Xunzhou (勋州), a jimi prefecture split from Yingzhou under Zangzhou (later Qianzhou) Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_xunzhou.etymology_analysis: Xunzhou (勋州, 'merit prefecture') was established in 655 CE as a Tang jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command.

b_houzhou.first_mention_attestation: Established in 641 CE (15th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Houzhou (候州/侯州), a jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_houzhou.etymology_analysis: Houzhou (侯州/候州) was established in 641 CE as a Tang jimi prefecture under Qianzhou Area Command in the Guizhou frontier (modern Guiding area).

b_dushang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 629 CE (3rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Dushang County under Yingzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_dushang.etymology_analysis: Dushang (都尚) was established in 629 CE in East Xie (东谢) territory in southern Guizhou (modern Duyun area), likely a sinicized transcription of a local Kra-Dai/Miao toponym.

b_tuolong.first_mention_attestation: Established in 629 CE (3rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Tuolong County under Yingzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
b_tuolong.etymology_analysis: Tuolong (陁隆) was established in 629 CE as a county of Yingzhou in East Xie territory (modern Taijiang/Qiandongnan area, Guizhou), likely rendering a local indigenous place name.

b_yingjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 629 CE (3rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Yingjiang County under Yingzhou (abolished in 655 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).
