b_yingjiang.etymology_analysis: Yingjiang (应江) was established in 629 CE under Yingzhou in southern Guizhou (modern Pingtang County), named after the local river associated with Yingzhou.

b_hanyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 602 CE (2nd year of Renshou, Sui dynasty) as Hanyuan Garrison (upgraded to Hanyuan County in 604 CE), named after the Hanchuan River, recorded in Suishu and Hanyuan County Gazetteer.
b_hanyuan.etymology_analysis: Hanyuan (汉源, 'source of the Han [River]') was established by the Sui dynasty in 602–604 CE and named after the Hanchuan River (modern Liusha River) in western Sichuan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shiji and Hanshu: Zuodu was established as Maoniu County under Shenli Commandery in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han).
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Zuodu in pre-Han times and Maoniu County from 111 BCE before Sui established Hanyuan in 602–604 CE.

b_tongwang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tang administrative records (668 CE / Kaiyuan–Zhenyuan era) as Tongwang County under Lizhou, renamed from Yangshan County, and recorded in Manshu (Vol. 1) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_tongwang.etymology_analysis: Tongwang (通望, 'clear lookout') was a Tang-era frontier county on the Dadu River (modern Dashu Town, Hanyuan County), renamed from Yangshan County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang administrative records for Lizhou: Yangshan County existed prior to its renaming as Tongwang County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Yangshan County before being renamed Tongwang County in the Tang dynasty.

b_longyou.first_mention_attestation: Named Longyou County in 590 CE (10th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), renamed from Qingyi County after a dragon sighting in the river during the conquest of Chen, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29).
b_longyou.etymology_analysis: Longyou (龙游, 'dragon swimming') was bestowed by Sui Wendi in 590 CE when a dragon was reportedly seen swimming in the river near Qingyi County (modern Leshan, Sichuan).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Hanshu: known as Qingyi in Western Han, Emei County under Northern Zhou, and Qingyi again in 589 CE before becoming Longyou in 590 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Continuously occupied since Western Han as Qingyi, renamed Emei in Northern Zhou and Longyou in 590 CE.

b_jiajiang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 593 CE (13th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) as Jiajiang County from parts of Pingqiang and Longyou counties, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_jiajiang.etymology_analysis: Jiajiang (夹江, 'flanked river') was established in 593 CE and named for its location along the Qingyi River where two mountains face each other across the stream.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi and Jiajiang County records: Han Nan'an County territory, where Northern Zhou established Pingqiang County in 561 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Carved out of Northern Zhou Pingqiang County (561 CE) and Longyou County in 593 CE.

b_suishan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 615 CE (11th year of Daye, Sui dynasty; 614/615 CE) as Suishan County under Meishan Commandery, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_suishan.etymology_analysis: Suishan (绥山) was established by the Sui dynasty in 615 CE at Rongle City to pacify local Liao tribes, taking its name from nearby Mount Sui (modern Suishan Town, Emeishan City).

b_qianwei.first_mention_attestation: Named Qianwei County in 583 CE (3rd year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Wuyang County was renamed Qianwei, inheriting the name of Han-era Qianwei Commandery (135 BCE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29).
b_qianwei.etymology_analysis: Qianwei (犍为) derives from the Western Han Qianwei Commandery (135 BCE); in 583 CE, the Sui dynasty renamed Northern Zhou's Wuyang County to Qianwei County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Qianwei County records: Northern Zhou established Wuyang County in 563 CE (Baoding 3) before Sui renamed it Qianwei in 583 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Wuyang County (563 CE) under Chenxi Commandery before being renamed Qianwei in 583 CE.

b_tongyi.first_mention_attestation: Named Tongyi County in 601 CE (1st year of Renshou, Sui dynasty) when Guangtong County was renamed Tongyi, serving as seat of Meizhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_tongyi.etymology_analysis: Tongyi (通义, 'comprehensive righteousness') was bestowed by the Sui dynasty in 601 CE on the seat of Meizhou (modern Meishan, Sichuan), replacing Guangtong.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu and Meizhou records: known as Qitong under Liang/Northern Zhou and renamed Guangtong in early Kaihuang before becoming Tongyi in 601 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier known as Qitong and Guangtong before 601 CE.

b_danling.first_mention_attestation: Named Danling County in 593 CE (13th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty; 592 CE per Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi) when the original Hongya County was renamed Danling, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29).
b_danling.etymology_analysis: Danling (丹棱, 'cinnabar ridge') was named by the Sui dynasty in 593 CE after the reddish ridges in the county when Hongya County was split and renamed.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Danling County records: originally Hongya County before 593 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Hongya County until 593 CE, when Hongya was moved south and the old seat became Danling.

b_hongya.first_mention_attestation: Established at its current site in 593 CE (13th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty; 592 CE per Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi) as Hongya County, upgraded from Northern Zhou's Hongya Garrison, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_hongya.etymology_analysis: Hongya (洪雅) was established as a Northern Zhou garrison and upgraded to a county in 593 CE on the Qingyi River in central Sichuan.

b_nuozuo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) as Nuozuozhou (诺祚州), one of the 46 Tang jimi tribal prefectures established in the Songzhou/Xizhou frontier region during the Zhenguan–Yonghui era (mid-7th century CE).
b_nuozuo.etymology_analysis: Nuozuo (诺祚) is a Tang-era Chinese phonetic transcription of a Qiangic or Tibeto-Burman tribal/place name in the western Sichuan frontier (modern Liangshan/Aba).

b_beilu_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) as Beiluzhou (卑卢州), one of the 46 Tang jimi tribal prefectures in the Songzhou/Xizhou frontier region during the Zhenguan–Yonghui era (mid-7th century CE).
b_beilu_2.etymology_analysis: Beilu (卑卢) is a Tang-era Chinese phonetic transcription of a Qiangic or Tibeto-Burman tribal/place name recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b).

b_baosai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Manshu (Vol. 1, 864 CE) and Tang records of 794 CE (10th year of Zhenyuan), when Xichuan Jiedushi forces and Nanzhao captured Baosai City (保塞城), formerly Liuqiang Garrison (柳强镇) before the Tianbao era.
b_baosai.etymology_analysis: Baosai (保塞, 'protecting the frontier pass') was a strategic Tang/Tibetan fortress north of Taideng in Xizhou (modern Liangshan, Sichuan), recaptured by Tang and Nanzhao forces in 794 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Manshu (Vol. 1): 'Baosai City... prior to Tianbao (742 CE) was Liuqiang Garrison of Xizhou.'
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Liuqiang Garrison prior to the Tianbao era (742 CE) before being fortified as Baosai City.

b_linqiong.first_mention_attestation: Founded and walled in 311 BCE by Qin general Zhang Yi and Shu governor Zhang Ruo alongside Chengdu and Pi, recorded in Huayang Guozhi and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_linqiong.etymology_analysis: Linqiong (临邛, 'overlooking Qiong') was one of the three earliest Qin-walled cities in Shu (311 BCE), named for its position overlooking the Qiong River and Qionglai Mountains (modern Qionglai, Sichuan).

b_pujiang.first_mention_attestation: Named Pujiang County in 601 CE (1st year of Renshou, Sui dynasty) when Guangding County was renamed Pujiang after the Pujiang River, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_pujiang.etymology_analysis: Pujiang (蒲江, 'cattail river') was named in 601 CE after the Pujiang River flowing south of the county seat.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31): Western Wei Emperor Gongdi (554–556 CE) established Guangding County, renamed Pujiang in 601 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Guangding County in Western Wei (554–556 CE) before being renamed Pujiang in 601 CE.

b_huojing.first_mention_attestation: Established in the Western Wei/Northern Zhou era (c. 553–581 CE) as Huojing County (named after the ancient natural gas 'fire well' at Linqiong), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_huojing.etymology_analysis: Huojing (火井, 'fire well') is named after the famous natural gas seep/well in Linqiong (modern Qionglai), attested since the Han dynasty and made a county seat in Western Wei/Northern Zhou.

b_yandao.first_mention_attestation: Established in 316 BCE (or 285 BCE under Shu Commandery) by the Qin dynasty as Yandao County, recorded in Hanshu and Sichuan historical gazetteers.
b_yandao.etymology_analysis: Yandao (严道) was a Qin-era frontier county ('dao', a Han/Qin administrative unit for non-Han borderlands) guarding the steep pass into western Sichuan (modern Yingjing/Ya'an).

b_rongjing.first_mention_attestation: Established in 620 CE (3rd year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Rongjing County under Yazhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao.
b_rongjing.etymology_analysis: Rongjing (荣经, later written 荥经 Yingjing in Ming) was established in 620 CE under Yazhou, named after the Rong and Jing rivers converging in the valley.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Qin/Han Yandao County seat was located in modern Yingjing County before Tang established Rongjing County in 620 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: The ancient Qin–Han Yandao County site lies in modern Yingjing County.

b_baizhang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 634 CE (8th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Baizhang County under Yazhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) and Manshu (Vol. 1).
b_baizhang_1.etymology_analysis: Baizhang (百丈, 'hundred zhang') was established in 634 CE as a county and post station under Yazhou (modern Mingshan/Ya'an, Sichuan), named after the tall Mount Baizhang.

b_chengdu.first_mention_attestation: Walled in 311 BCE by Qin general Zhang Yi and Shu governor Zhang Ruo as Chengdu, following the Qin conquest of Shu in 316 BCE, recorded in Shiji and Huayang Guozhi.
b_chengdu.etymology_analysis: Chengdu (成都, 'becoming a capital') is the ancient capital of the Shu state and Sichuan, traditionally explained by the Shu king's saying that 'in one year it became a town, in two years a city, in three years a capital (chengdu).'

b_wenjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established in the late Western Wei (c. 553–556 CE) as Wenjiang County under Shu Commandery (later Wanchun in 603 CE, restored as Wenjiang in 627 CE), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_wenjiang.etymology_analysis: Wenjiang (温江, 'warm river') was named after the Wenjiang (Min River distributary) flowing past the county seat, first established in Western Wei (c. 553–556 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31): briefly named Wanchun County in 603 CE (Renshou 3) before reverting to Wenjiang in 627 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Temporarily named Wanchun County from 603 CE to 627 CE.

b_xinfan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Xinfan County during the Northern Zhou (557–581 CE) from Han-era Fan County (繁县), and re-established in 620 CE (Wude 3), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_xinfan.etymology_analysis: Xinfan (新繁, 'new Fan') was renamed by the Northern Zhou from the Western Han Fan County (which itself was named after the Fan River) on the Chengdu Plain.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31): Western Han Fan County under Shu Commandery.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Fan County (繁县) in Western Han before being renamed Xinfan in Northern Zhou.

b_luo.first_mention_attestation: Established in Western Han (201 BCE, 6th year of Gaozu) as Luo County (雒县) under Guanghan Commandery, named after the Luo River, recorded in Hanshu and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_luo.etymology_analysis: Luo (雒) is a Western Han county (201 BCE) named after the Luo River (雒水) flowing south of the city (modern Guanghan, Sichuan).

b_mianzhu.first_mention_attestation: Established in Western Han (c. 201 BCE) as Mianzhu County under Guanghan Commandery, recorded in Hanshu and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_mianzhu.etymology_analysis: Mianzhu (绵竹) is a Western Han county named for the Mian River (绵水) and the abundant bamboo groves along its banks.

b_deyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in the Eastern Han (c. 130 CE, split from Mianzhu County under Guanghan Commandery) as Deyang County, and re-established in 620 CE (Wude 3), recorded in Hou Hanshu and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_deyang.etymology_analysis: Deyang (德阳) was established in the Eastern Han dynasty (c. 130 CE) from Mianzhu County, bearing an auspicious name meaning 'virtuous yang.'

b_yangan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yang'an County in 553 CE (2nd year of Fei of Western Wei) from Han-era Niupi County (牛鞞县), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31).
b_yangan.etymology_analysis: Yang'an (阳安) was established in 553 CE by Western Wei when it renamed the ancient Han county of Niupi (modern Jianyang, Sichuan), serving as the seat of Jianzhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 31): Western Han Niupi County under Qianwei Commandery, renamed Yang'an in 553 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Niupi County (牛鞞县) from Western Han until 553 CE.

b_jinshui.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jinshui County in 618 CE (1st year of Wude, Tang dynasty) from Jinyuan County (金渊县) to observe the naming taboo of Emperor Gaozu (Li Yuan), recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_jinshui.etymology_analysis: Jinshui (金水, 'gold water') was renamed from Jinyuan (金渊) in 618 CE to avoid the personal name taboo of Tang Emperor Gaozu (Li Yuan, 渊).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jintang/Jianzhou records: Western Wei established Jinyuan County in 553 CE, renamed Jinshui in 618 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Jinyuan County (553 CE) before the 618 CE taboo renaming.

b_renshou.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Renshou County in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) from Puning County (普宁县), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29).
b_renshou.etymology_analysis: Renshou (仁寿, 'benevolence and longevity') is an auspicious name bestowed by the Sui dynasty in 598 CE on Puning County, serving as the seat of Lingzhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29): originally Puning County (Western Wei, 553 CE) before being renamed Renshou in 598 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Puning County (553 CE) until 598 CE.

b_jingyan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 591 CE (11th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) as Jingyan County, replacing Puting County (蒲亭县), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jingyan County Historical Records.
b_jingyan.etymology_analysis: Jingyan (井研) was established in 591 CE under Lingzhou, named after its local salt wells (traditionally associated with the Yan/Yanjing salt well).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jingyan County Historical Records: Western Wei established Puting County in 553 CE, replaced by Jingyan County in 591 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Puting County (553 CE) before being replaced by Jingyan County in 591 CE.

b_wenshan.first_mention_attestation: Named Wenshan County in 280 CE (6th year of Xianning, Western Jin dynasty) when Miansi County (绵虒县) was renamed Wenshan, later serving as seat of Maozhou, recorded in Jinshu and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi.
b_wenshan.etymology_analysis: Wenshan (汶山, anciently interchangeable with Minshan 岷山) was named in 280 CE after the Min Mountains of the upper Min River valley, serving as the seat of Maozhou (modern Mao County, Sichuan).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu and Wenchuan County records: Western Han established Wenshan Commandery and Miansi County in 111 BCE, renamed Wenshan County in 280 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Miansi County (111 BCE) before being renamed Wenshan County in 280 CE.

b_tonghua.first_mention_attestation: Established in 624 CE (7th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Tonghua County under Weizhou/Maozhou, located near Northern Zhou's Shimen Garrison, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 32).
b_tonghua.etymology_analysis: Tonghua (通化, 'thorough civilizing transformation') was a Tang-era frontier county in the upper Min River valley under Maozhou/Weizhou (modern Li/Mao County area, Sichuan).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 32): Northern Zhou Emperor Wu established Shimen Garrison (石门镇) at the site prior to Tonghua County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Shimen Garrison (Northern Zhou, c. 561–578 CE) prior to the Tang county of Tonghua.

b_yishui_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yishui County (翼水县) in the Sui dynasty (Suishu, Geography Treatise), initially under Wenshan Commandery / Huizhou, and transferred to Yizhou (翼州) in 618 CE (Jiu Tangshu, Vol. 41; Xin Tangshu, Vol. 42).
b_yishui_2.etymology_analysis: Yishui (翼水) is named after the local Yi River (翼水), a tributary in the upper Min River basin in northern Sichuan.

b_jiulong.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jiulong County (九陇县) in the Sui dynasty (Suishu, Geography Treatise), becoming the seat of Pengzhou in 686 CE (Jiu Tangshu, Vol. 41; Xin Tangshu, Vol. 42).
b_jiulong.etymology_analysis: Jiulong (九陇, 'Nine Ridges') takes its name from the nine mountain ridges in the area north of the Chengdu Plain.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41), noting Jiulong occupied the territory of Han-era Fan County (繁县) and Liu Song-era Jinshou Commandery (晋寿郡)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Fan County and Liu Song-era Jinshou Commandery preceded the Sui-era establishment of Jiulong County in the same locality.

b_daojiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Daojiang County (导江县) in 618 CE (1st year of Wude, Tang dynasty) from Panlong County, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_daojiang.etymology_analysis: Daojiang (导江, 'guiding the river') refers to the ancient Dujiangyan hydraulic works that channel the Min River onto the Chengdu Plain, echoing the Shangshu phrase 'Minshan daojiang' (岷山导江).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Shu Han records, noting Shu Han established Du'an County, Northern Zhou renamed it Wenshan, and Tang briefly called it Panlong in 618 CE before renaming it Daojiang
older_name_by_867.notes: Succeeded Shu Han Du'an County and Northern Zhou Wenshan County on the same Dujiangyan/Guankou site.

b_huacheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Huacheng County (化成县 / 化城县) in the Southern Liang and Northern Wei period (c. 505–514 CE) as the seat of Bazhou and Dagu Commandery, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_huacheng.etymology_analysis: Huacheng (化成/化城) is an auspicious administrative name meaning 'city of civilizing transformation,' serving as the prefectural seat of Bazhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hou Hanshu and Bazhou local gazetteer records, noting Eastern Han established Hanchang County here in 109 CE (Yongchu 3)
older_name_by_867.notes: Eastern Han Hanchang County (109 CE) was the direct predecessor of Huacheng County at modern Bazhong.

b_qizhang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zengkou County (曾口县) from the Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) under Bazhou.
b_qizhang.etymology_analysis: Per b_origin/b_hanzi, this barony represents Zengkou (曾口, 'mouth of the Zeng'), named for its location at the mouth of the Zengkou Valley/stream, a settlement compound.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Songshu and Bazhou historical records, noting Liu Song established Guihua Commandery at Zengkou Valley in 447 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Guihua Commandery was established at Zengkou Valley under Liu Song before Zengkou County was constituted under Southern Liang.

b_guiren.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Guiren County (归仁县) in the Sui dynasty (Suishu, Vol. 29, Qinghua Commandery) and Tang dynasty (Jiu Tangshu, Vol. 39, Bazhou).
b_guiren.etymology_analysis: Guiren (归仁, 'returning to benevolence') is an auspicious imperial administrative name given in the Sui dynasty.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39), noting Southern Liang established Pingzhou before Sui renamed it Guiren County
older_name_by_867.notes: Southern Liang Pingzhou was reorganized and renamed Guiren County by the Sui dynasty.

b_kaijiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Kaijiang County (开江县) in 763 CE (1st year of Guangde, Tang dynasty) from Shengshan County due to a naming taboo, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_kaijiang.etymology_analysis: Kaijiang (开江) was named after the local Kai River (开江, modern Nanhe) in 763 CE when Shengshan County was renamed to avoid a homophone taboo with 'Sheng' (圣).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Taiping Huanyu Ji (Vol. 137), noting Yongning County was renamed Shengshan in 598 CE and Kaijiang in 763 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Formerly Yongning County, renamed Shengshan County in 598 CE, and renamed Kaijiang County in 763 CE (distinct from modern Kaijiang County in Sichuan, which was Xinning until 1914).

b_xinpu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Xinpu County (新浦县) from the Western Wei / Northern Zhou period (553–581 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) under Kaizhou.
b_xinpu.etymology_analysis: Xinpu (新浦, 'new riverbank/creek') is a settlement compound designating the newly established county seat along the river in Kaizhou.

b_liujiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liujiang County (流江县) in 522 CE (3rd year of Putong, Southern Liang dynasty) alongside North Dangqu Commandery, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Qu County records.
b_liujiang.etymology_analysis: Liujiang (流江, 'flowing river') was named after the local river (modern Qu River) flowing past the county seat of Quzhou.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Huayang Guozhi, recording Qin/Han Dangqu County in the same region
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Dangqu County lay nearby in the Qu River valley before Southern Liang established Liujiang County in 522 CE.

b_linshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Linshui County (潾水县, later written 邻水县) in 537 CE (3rd year of Datong, Southern Liang dynasty), recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Taiping Huanyu Ji.
b_linshui.etymology_analysis: Linshui (潾水) is named after the clear mountain stream (潾水 / 邻水) flowing through the county in eastern Sichuan.

b_qujiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qujiang County (渠江县) in August 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Shi'an County, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_qujiang.etymology_analysis: Qujiang (渠江) is named after the Qu River (渠江) that flows past the county seat (modern Guang'an).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39) and Suishu (Vol. 29), noting Southern Liang established Shi'an County (522 CE), renamed Bincheng in 598 CE, restored to Shi'an in 618 CE, and renamed Qujiang in 742 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Southern Liang Shi'an County (522 CE), briefly Sui Bincheng County (598–618 CE), before being renamed Qujiang County in 742 CE.

b_tongchuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tongchuan County (通川县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) from Shicheng County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_tongchuan_1.etymology_analysis: Tongchuan (通川, 'through-flowing valley/stream') was the Sui-era renaming of Shicheng County, serving as the seat of Tongzhou (modern Dazhou).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Tongchuan Commandery records, noting Southern Liang established Shicheng County as seat of Dongguan Commandery
older_name_by_867.notes: Southern Liang Shicheng County was renamed Tongchuan County in 598 CE.

b_baqu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Baqu County (巴渠县) in 765 CE (1st year of Yongtai, Tang dynasty) by splitting four townships from Shigu County, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Taiping Huanyu Ji (Vol. 137).
b_baqu.etymology_analysis: Baqu (巴渠) is named after the Baqu River (巴渠江) flowing through the area in eastern Sichuan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Suishu (Vol. 29), recording that Baqu was carved out of Western Wei-era Shigu County in 765 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Carved out of Shigu County (established under Western Wei) in 765 CE.

b_dongxiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dongxiang (东乡) from 96 CE (8th year of Yongyuan, Eastern Han) and as Dongxiang County (东乡县) from the Western Wei period (553 CE), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xuanhan County records.
b_dongxiang.etymology_analysis: Dongxiang (东乡, 'eastern township') originated as an Eastern Han administrative district name (96 CE) and became a county under Western Wei, retaining the name until 1914 when it was renamed Xuanhan.

b_yongmu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yongmu County (永穆县) from the Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) under Tongzhou.
b_yongmu.etymology_analysis: Yongmu (永穆, 'eternal harmony/solemnity') is an auspicious administrative name established under the Southern Liang dynasty.

b_nanchong.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Nanchong County (南充县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) from Anhan County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_nanchong.etymology_analysis: Nanchong (南充) derives from its position relative to the ancient Chongguo (充国) territory when Sui renamed Anhan County in 598 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Suishu (Vol. 29), noting Anhan County was established in Western Han and renamed Nanchong in 598 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Western Han Anhan County was the direct predecessor on the same site until 598 CE.

b_xiangru.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xiangru County (相如县) in the Northern Zhou dynasty (557–581 CE) after abolishing Southern Liang's Zitong Commandery, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42).
b_xiangru.etymology_analysis: Xiangru (相如) is named after the Western Han poet Sima Xiangru (司马相如, 179–117 BCE), whose ancestral residence and lute terrace (相如故宅) were located 20 li south of the county seat per Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41), stating Xiangru was carved from Han-era Anhan County territory
older_name_by_867.notes: Carved out of Han-era Anhan County territory; Southern Liang placed Zitong Commandery here before Northern Zhou established Xiangru County.

b_hanchu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hanchu County (汉初县) from the Southern Liang dynasty (c. 507 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 42) under Guozhou.
b_hanchu.etymology_analysis: Hanchu (汉初, 'early Han') is a Southern Liang-era county name in the Jialing River valley, preserved until its merger into Nanchong in 1283 CE (modern Wusheng County).

b_langzhong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Langzhong County (阆中县) in 314 BCE after Qin conquered Ba, recorded in Shiji, Hanshu (Geography Treatise), and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_langzhong.etymology_analysis: Langzhong (阆中) means 'amidst the lofty/encircling mountains and winding Lang River,' as explained in Taiping Huanyu Ji ('its mountains enclose the commandery on four sides') and Jiu Tangshu ('the Lang River winds around three sides of the commandery').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and Suishu (Vol. 29), noting Sui renamed Langzhong to Langnei (581–618 CE) to avoid a naming taboo
older_name_by_867.notes: Langzhong is the original Qin name (314 BCE); Sui temporarily renamed it Langnei (581–618 CE) before Tang restored Langzhong.

b_cangxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Cangxi County (苍溪县) in the Western Jin dynasty (265–316 CE) under Baxi Commandery, recorded in Jinshu (Geography Treatise) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41).
b_cangxi.etymology_analysis: Cangxi (苍溪, 'deep-green brook') is named after a local stream/valley in the upper Jialing River basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Dushi Fangyu Jiyao and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41), noting Southern Qi renamed it Hanchang before Sui restored Cangxi in 598 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Western Jin Cangxi County was temporarily renamed Hanchang under Southern Qi and Liang, then restored to Cangxi in 598 CE.

b_nanbu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Nanbu County (南部县) in 503 CE (2nd year of Tianjian, Southern Liang dynasty) from Nanguo County, recorded in Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41) and local gazetteers.
b_nanbu.etymology_analysis: Nanbu (南部, 'southern division') is an administrative name given in 503 CE when Southern Liang reorganized the southern part of Chongguo/Nanchongguo.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 41), recording Western Han Chongguo County, Jin Nanchongguo, and Liu Song Nanguo
older_name_by_867.notes: Succeeded Western Han Chongguo County and Liu Song Nanguo County on the same site.

b_miangu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Miangu County (绵谷县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) from Xing'an County as the seat of Lizhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Jiu Tangshu (Vol. 39).
b_miangu.etymology_analysis: Miangu (绵谷) refers to the winding mountain valley at Guangyuan where the Jialing River emerges from the Qinling-Daba passes.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Lizhou historical records, noting Western Wei/Northern Zhou seat was Xing'an County until 598 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Xing'an County served as the seat of Lizhou before being renamed Miangu County in 598 CE.

b_jinggu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jinggu County (景谷县) from the Sui dynasty (Suishu, Vol. 29, Yicheng Commandery) and Tang dynasty (Xin Tangshu, Vol. 40, Lizhou).
b_jinggu.etymology_analysis: Jinggu (景谷, 'bright/scenic valley') is a valley toponym in the northern Sichuan mountains near the Bailong/Jialing confluence.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Suishu (Vol. 29), noting Jinggu occupied the territory of Han-era Baishui County
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Baishui County was located in the same valley system before Sui-era Jinggu County.

b_jiameng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiameng County (葭萌县) in the Qin dynasty (314 BCE) / Western Han, recorded in Shiji, Hanshu (Geography Treatise), and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_jiameng.etymology_analysis: Jiameng (葭萌) was an ancient Ba-Shu settlement name (attested in Qin-Han records as a marquisate/county) at the strategic Jialing-Bailong confluence.

b_pengchi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Pengchi County (蓬池县) in 763 CE (1st year of Guangde, Tang dynasty) from Dayin County as the seat of Pengzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_pengchi.etymology_analysis: Pengchi (蓬池) was named after Pengzhou (蓬州) and a local pool when Dayin County was renamed in 763 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40), noting Southern Liang established Dayin County, which became Pengzhou's seat in 741 CE and was renamed Pengchi in 763 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Southern Liang Dayin County (502–557 CE), renamed Pengchi County in 763 CE.

b_fuyu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fuyu County (伏虞县) from the Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) under Pengzhou.
b_fuyu.etymology_analysis: Fuyu (伏虞) is a Southern Liang-era administrative name in eastern Sichuan under Pengzhou.

b_qushui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Qushui County (曲水县) from the Western Wei dynasty (c. 553 CE) as the seat of Wenzhou / Yinping Commandery, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_qushui.etymology_analysis: Qushui (曲水, 'winding river') refers to the meandering course of the Bailong/Baishui River through modern Wen County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hanshu (Geography Treatise) and Suishu (Vol. 29), recording Han-era Yinping Circuit/County in the same locality
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Yinping (阴平) was the ancient predecessor in the Wen County basin before Western Wei established Qushui County.

b_tongchang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tongchang County (同昌县) from the Western Wei / Northern Zhou period (c. 553–581 CE) and in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) under Fuzhou.
b_tongchang.etymology_analysis: Tongchang (同昌, 'prospering together') is an auspicious Northern Zhou/Western Wei administrative name in the Fuzhou/Wenzhou borderlands.

b_tongjiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tongjiang County (通江县) in 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Nuoshui County as the seat of Bizhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Taiping Huanyu Ji.
b_tongjiang.etymology_analysis: Tongjiang (通江) is named after the Tongjiang River (通江, formed by the confluence of the Nuoshui and other mountain streams).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40), stating Tongjiang was originally Nuoshui County (established in Western Wei/Northern Zhou, restored in 625 CE) before being renamed in 742 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Nuoshui County was the seat of Bizhou from 625 CE until it was renamed Tongjiang County in 742 CE.

b_baishi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Baishi County (白石县) in the Western Wei Feidi period (c. 553 CE) under Dongba Prefecture (later Jizhou), recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_baishi.etymology_analysis: Baishi (白石, 'white stone') is a settlement compound named for prominent white limestone/rock formations in the area (modern Shaxi Town, Tongjiang County).

b_dongba.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Dongba County (东巴县) in 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Taiping County under Bizhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_dongba.etymology_analysis: Dongba (东巴, 'Eastern Ba') was the 742 CE Tang renaming of Taiping County, located in the eastern Ba region (modern Huangzhong Town, Wanyuan).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40), recording Taiping County was established in 735 CE (23rd year of Kaiyuan) and renamed Dongba in 742 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Taiping County in 735 CE and renamed Dongba County seven years later in 742 CE.

b_fuyang_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fuyang County (符阳县) from the Northern Wei Zhengshi era (504–508 CE) under Qizhang Commandery, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_fuyang_2.etymology_analysis: Fuyang (符阳) is an administrative settlement name established under Northern Wei, located at modern Fuyang Town in Tongjiang County.

b_nanjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanjiang County (难江县) in the Northern Zhou dynasty (557–581 CE) as the seat of Pingsang Commandery / Jizhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_nanjiang.etymology_analysis: Nanjiang (难江, 'treacherous river') was named after the steep, difficult-to-navigate Nanjiang River in the Daba Mountains; in the Qing dynasty it was renamed Nanjiang (南江, 'South River').

b_jiachuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jiachuan County (嘉川县) in the Sui dynasty (Suishu, Vol. 29, Yicheng Commandery) and Tang dynasty (Xin Tangshu, Vol. 40, Lizhou/Jizhou).
b_jiachuan.etymology_analysis: Jiachuan (嘉川, 'fine stream') is named after the Jiachuan River valley in modern Wangcang County, northern Sichuan.

b_nanzheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Nanzheng (南郑) from the Warring States period (451 BCE in Zhushu Jinian / Shiji) and established as a Qin county in 312 BCE, recorded in Shiji, Hanshu, and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_nanzheng.etymology_analysis: Nanzheng (南郑, 'Southern Zheng') is traditionally explained in Shuijingzhu as a settlement founded by refugees from the State of Zheng who migrated south into the Hanzhong Basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Hanzhong records, noting Western Wei renamed Nanzheng to Guangyi (554–605 CE) before Sui restored Nanzheng
older_name_by_867.notes: Nanzheng is the ancient Warring States/Qin name; it was temporarily called Guangyi from 554 to 605 CE.

b_xi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Xi County (西县) in 607 CE (3rd year of Daye, Sui dynasty) from Bozhong County, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 29) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) under Xingyuan Prefecture.
b_xi.etymology_analysis: Xi County (西县, 'Western County') was named in 607 CE for its location in the western Hanzhong Basin (modern Mian County, Shaanxi).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Suishu (Vol. 29) and Liangzhou records, noting Northern Wei established Bozhong County before Sui renamed it Xi County in 607 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Northern Wei Bozhong County (named after Mount Bozhong) was renamed Xi County in 607 CE.

b_sanquan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Sanquan County (三泉县) in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) by splitting Miangu County as the seat of Nan'an Prefecture, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_sanquan.etymology_analysis: Sanquan (三泉, 'Three Springs') is named after the three natural springs at its original site in modern Ningqiang County, Shaanxi.

b_chenggu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chenggu County (城固县 / 成固县) in the Qin/Western Han period (312–202 BCE), recorded in Hanshu (Geography Treatise), Suishu (Vol. 29), and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_chenggu.etymology_analysis: Chenggu (城固, 'fortified and firm') is a Qin-Han strategic fortress name in the eastern Hanzhong Basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Liangzhou / Xin Tangshu records, noting Chenggu was briefly renamed Tanggu from 619 to 628 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Chenggu is the original Qin-Han name; it was briefly called Tanggu (619–628 CE) in the early Tang before reverting to Chenggu.

b_xingdao.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Xingdao County (兴道县) in 649 CE (23rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) from Xingshi County, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao.
b_xingdao.etymology_analysis: Xingdao (兴道, 'flourishing way') was the 649 CE Tang renaming of Xingshi County, serving as the seat of Yangzhou from 756 CE (modern Yang County, Shaanxi).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Dushi Fangyu Jiyao and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40), noting Northern Wei established Xingshi County in 514 CE (Yanchang 3), renamed Xingdao in 649 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Northern Wei Xingshi County (514 CE), named after Mount Xingshi, was renamed Xingdao County in 649 CE.

b_xixiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Xixiang County (西乡县) in 281 CE (2nd year of Taikang, Western Jin dynasty) from Nanxiang County, recorded in Jinshu (Geography Treatise) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40).
b_xixiang.etymology_analysis: Xixiang (西乡, 'western township') was renamed from Shu Han's Nanxiang County in 281 CE by Western Jin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Dushi Fangyu Jiyao and Xixiang County records, noting Shu Han established Nanxiang County (221 CE), Jin renamed it Xixiang (281 CE), and Western Wei briefly called it Fengning before Sui restored Xixiang in 607 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Succeeded Shu Han's Nanxiang County (221 CE); temporarily renamed Fengning under Western Wei/Northern Zhou.

b_zhenfu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zhenfu County (真符县) in 749 CE (8th year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Huayang County after an auspicious Daoist tally discovery, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Yangzhou records.
b_zhenfu.etymology_analysis: Zhenfu (真符, 'true tally') was given in 749 CE when Tang Xuanzong renamed Huayang County to commemorate an auspicious Daoist jade tally.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 40) and Yangzhou historical records, noting Huayang County was established in 730 CE (18th year of Kaiyuan) and renamed Zhenfu in 749 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Huayang County (established 730 CE, re-established 748 CE) was renamed Zhenfu County in 749 CE.
